Colorado State.title: A new era begins: Joel and Mike discuss Jim Mora, the Border War and a different-looking CSU football program
Colorado State.summary:
This RamNation Radio episode is brought to you by Pedersen Toyota, your Local Toyota Dealer Serving Fort Collins, Loveland, Windsor and Timnath for more than 50 years. It is also made possible by Ginger and Baker — our favorite restaurant(s) in all of Fort Collins, and Ram Zone (powered by the CSU Bookstore) — the best place to get all your Ram gear.

With kickoff finally here, Joel and Mike look ahead to Jim Mora’s CSU debut and a Border War matchup that could immediately set the tone for a new era of Rams football. They break down an offseason of massive change in Fort Collins, from CSU’s move to the Pac-12 and new Adidas uniforms to a revamped roster and an athletic department that appears more committed than ever to building a winning football program. The guys discuss what they’ll be watching for against Wyoming, including CSU’s still-unannounced starting quarterback, whether 60+ new players can come together quickly, the battle in the trenches, and whether Mora’s emphasis on discipline and attention to detail will finally produce a cleaner, tougher football team. They also make their predictions for the Border War and define what would make Mora’s first season a success. Plus, after last week’s memorable conversation with Jim McElwain, Joel and Mike look back at some of their favorite guests and moments from six years of RamNation Radio.

Colorado State.title: Jim McElwain returns: Rebuilding CSU, legendary wins and why he believes in Jim Mora
Colorado State.summary:
This 200th RamNation Radio episode is brought to you by Pedersen Toyota, your Local Toyota Dealer Serving Fort Collins, Loveland, Windsor and Timnath for more than 50 years. It is also made possible by Ginger and Baker — our favorite restaurant(s) in all of Fort Collins, and Ram Zone (powered by the CSU Bookstore) — the best place to get all your Ram gear.

Former Colorado State head coach Jim McElwain joins RamNation Radio for a memorable look back at the era that produced CSU’s last 10-win season and last bowl victory. Coach Mac shares stories from taking over a struggling Rams program, why recruiting Colorado was so important, beating CU twice in three years, the unforgettable 2013 New Mexico Bowl comeback over Washington State, going toe-to-toe with No. 1 Alabama and the 2014 breakthrough that put CSU back on the national map. He also talks Garrett Grayson, Shaq Barrett, Rashard Higgins, the importance of the Border War and why he believed CSU deserved more respect nationally. Now retired, McElwain reflects on his return to Fort Collins and seeing Canvas Stadium for the first time, weighs in on today’s transfer portal and NIL-driven college football, laughs about some of the bizarre moments that followed him later in his career (i.e., Connor Stallions and the infamous shark photo), and explains why he thinks Jim Mora is a great fit to finally get the Rams winning again.

Gonzaga.title: Gonzaga scheduled to host Incarnate Word in fifth known home nonconference game
Gonzaga.summary:
Fans will have the opportunity to see Gonzaga no fewer than five times at McCarthey Athletic Center this season during the team’s nonconference schedule.

Gonzaga’s fifth known home nonconference game will take place on either Nov. 10 or 11 against Incarnate Word, according to Rocco Miller of Bracketeer.com. A tipoff time and television details for the Incarnate Word matchup, as well as Gonzaga’s four other home nonleague games, will be announced at a later date.

The Zags are squeezing the Incarnate Word game into the schedule between the Nov. 7 home opener against New Mexico State and a Nov. 14 matchup against LSU and first-year coach Will Wade at Numerica Veterans Arena.

It will be only the second meeting between Gonzaga and Incarnate Word, which lost 103-68 at the Kennel during the 2017-18 season. Rui Hachimura and Zach Norvell Jr. scored a combined 35 points off Gonzaga’s bench, with Josh Perkins adding 16 more points for the home team.

Incarnate Word is losing its top six scorers, including three players who averaged double digits, from last year’s team that finished 12-19 overall and ninth in the Southland Conference with a record of 7-15.

The Cardinals are 39-59 in three seasons under coach Shane Heirman, whose staff includes former Auburn, UTEP and Central Michigan coach Tony Barbee and former San Jose State coach Dave Wojcik, a longtime friend of Mark Few who once recruited ex-Zag standout Brandon Clarke to play for the Spartans in the Mountain West.

Aside from Incarnate Word and New Mexico State, the Zags are also scheduled to host Montana State (Nov. 17), NAIA Eastern Oregon (Dec. 2) and Cornell (Dec. 31) in home nonconference games.

The official nonconference schedule and full Pac-12 Conference schedule will be released within the next few weeks.

Gonzaga.title: Gonzaga returning to Climate Pledge Arena for nonleague games in 2026-27 and 2027-28
Gonzaga.summary:
Nonconference games at Climate Pledge Arena have been a fixture of Gonzaga’s schedules four of the last five seasons and the tradition will continue with a pair of matchups against Big Ten schools in 2026-27 and 2027-28.

The Zags will return to Seattle next year – and take a brief hiatus from their Pac-12 Conference schedule – to play Oregon on Jan. 30, according to Rocco Miller of Bracketeer.org. It will be the second game of a neutral-neutral series with Dana Altman’s program that started with Gonzaga’s 91-82 victory over the Ducks last season at Portland’s Moda Center.

A date hasn’t been set, but Gonzaga will make a pit stop at Climate Pledge during the 2027-28 season to play UCLA in a nonconference game, according to Miller. The West Coast powers renewed their rivalry this offseason, agreeing to another neutral-neutral series that will start this fall when the Zags travel to play the Bruins Dec. 5 at the Honda Center in Anaheim.

It’s been a mixed bag for Gonzaga in five games at Climate Pledge. Mark Few’s teams dropped the first three games they played in the building, losing 91-82 to Alabama in 2021, 76-63 to Connecticut in 2023 and 90-89 to Kentucky in an overtime matchup in 2024. The Zags finally broke their Climate Pledge spell last season with an 82-72 win over UCLA and returned roughly a month later to beat Seattle U 71-50 in West Coast Conference play.

With Oregon on the 2026-27 schedule, the Zags are guaranteed to play 10 nonconference games against high-major opponents and could face 11 if they advance to the championship game at the Players Era Festival in Las Vegas. Gonzaga will have at least two nonleague games wedged into its Pac-12 schedule, with a Feb. 20 meeting against Duke at Little Caesars Arena in Detroit.

Of the 18 players that played minutes in last year’s Gonzaga-Oregon matchup, just two are back on their respective rosters this season: the Zags’ Braden Huff and Ducks’ Sean Stewart.

Altman’s reloaded roster features freshman Tajh Ariza, the son of former NBA star Trevor Ariza and a four-star high school prospect who was considered one of the top 40 recruits in the country.

The Ducks lose top scorers Nate Bittle and Jackson Shelstad, but bring in a large group of high-impact transfers including San Francisco’s Tyrone Riley IV, Alabama’s Taylor Bol Bowen, Boise State’s Andrew Meadow, San Diego State’s Pharaoh Compton, Arizona’s Dwayne Aristode, Kentucky’s Jasper Johnson and Boston College’s Fred Payne.

Before last season’s meeting in Portland, Few had only matched up with his alma mater two other times since his Gonzaga tenure started in 1999. The Zags lost 70-64 to the Ducks during the Far West Classic in 1999 but edged Oregon 73-72 in overtime when the teams met in the Battle 4 Atlantis semifinals in 2019.

Last year’s matchup coincided with the season-high scoring performance of Gonzaga point guard Braeden Smith, who had 21 points on 7 of 10 shooting. Huff added 20 points while Graham Ike had 17 points and 11 rebounds. Oregon’s Bittle, a former GU recruit, led all scorers with 28 points to go with nine rebounds.

Gonzaga.title: Incoming Gonzaga guard Skylar Wicks decommits from program
Gonzaga.summary:
A day after landing a prized transfer, Gonzaga lost a veteran commit. And so the Zags’ roller-coaster offseason of recruiting continues.

Transfer guard Skylar Wicks, who pledged to Gonzaga’s basketball program in June, has decommitted and reopened his recruitment, according to a report from 247Sports.com.

Wicks’ decision comes a day after the Zags gained a commitment from transfer guard Xaivian Lee, who started 35 games last season at Florida.

Wicks played last season for Saint Francis, a Division I program in Pennsylvania, averaging 17.8 points, 6.7 rebounds, 2.8 assists and 1.4 steals per game. He then entered the transfer portal, seeking an additional season of eligibility after his career was disrupted by injuries. The 26-year-old was granted a seventh season earlier this month after the NCAA approved a waiver, clearing the way for Wicks to add experience to a new-look Zags backcourt.

The 6-foot-6 guard’s injury-riddled career has spanned five schools and four states. Wicks, a New Jersey native, began his career at Missouri State before stops at State College of Florida, Incarnate Word and Texas-San Antonio. He then had his most productive season last year at Saint Francis.

It was uncertain how Wicks would fit into the Zags’ rotation, but his commitment gave the team a potential contributor in the backcourt, which has had a whirlwind offseason, with players coming and going. Point guard Mario Saint-Supery opted to turn pro in Spain rather than returning to GU for his sophomore season. Incoming guard Jack Kayil kept his name in the NBA draft pool. Dayton transfer Javon Bennett committed to GU, but a court ruling has deemed the point guard ineligible for a fifth college season as of now.

Lee is currently eligible after a California judge granted a temporary restraining order against the NCAA, allowing the former Florida and Princeton star to pursue a fifth season of eligibility. GU’s backcourt also added Houston transfer Isiah Harwell and the team is still anticipating the arrival of Frenchman Nathan De Sousa, a 23-year-old point guard.

Gonzaga.title: Report: Florida transfer Xaivian Lee commits to Gonzaga
Gonzaga.summary:
From staff reports

Gonzaga lured its third 5-of-5 commitment when point guard Xaivian Lee orally committed Wednesday.

Lee made the announcement through social media on his Instagram page.

Lee played last season at Florida and the three previous seasons at Princeton. In his debut at Florida in 2025-26, Lee scored 14 points, had six rebounds and dished out five assists in a 93-87 loss to Arizona.

Earlier this month, Lee was granted a temporary restraining order against the NCAA and as a result was granted a fifth season of eligibility after filing a lawsuit in the state of California.

In three seasons at Princeton, Lee score 1,154 points with 406 rebounds, 302 assists, 124 made 3-pointers and 81 steals.

Gonzaga.title: Former Gonzaga standout Corey Kispert pours time into coffee company
Gonzaga.summary:
Corey Kispert wanted a name for his new business venture that represented the ups and downs associated with two passions in his life: Coffee and Basketball.

He chose The Bitter Truth for his coffee company that launched in March.

Kispert consumed a ton of coffee in four seasons at Gonzaga, but it wasn’t all sunshine and lollipops on the court in his first two years. He eventually figured it out and played a starring role on GU’s 31-1 squad that suffered its lone loss in the 2021 national championship against Baylor in Indianapolis.

“That’s been a reflection of my NBA career as well, a similar story and path (as Gonzaga),” said Kispert, who is entering his sixth NBA season. “I’ve learned a lot of I guess you’d call them bitter truths along the way, reflecting the struggle and hard times and adversity in my career and personal life aren’t something to run from.

“Even if you think you’re making strides, you’re not absent of issues that pop up. So work with them, stare them in the face and actually enjoy it and your life gets a lot easier. That’s kind of what the brand stands for – honest self-reflection and not lying to yourself.”

Kispert’s coffee infatuation began innocently enough as a high school senior in the Seattle area, percolated over four years as a Zag and brewed into his current daily ritual of 5-7 cups.

He grew up with “a Starbucks on every corner,” but his dad swore drinking coffee would stunt Corey’s growth until he got older. So Kispert waited a while. Having sprouted to 6-feet-6 and 210 pounds, he started eating breakfast during his senior year at King’s High with several buddies working construction who insisted on drinking straight black coffee.

“I did it in reverse,” Kispert said. “I wasn’t doing the triple vanilla macchiato people usually start with.”

Kispert met future wife Jenn Wirth, a standout on GU’s women’s basketball team, and she broadened his coffee horizons.

“Starbucks was the holy land to me, but she opened my eyes to the specialty shops,” he said. “On the road we do stay in nicer hotels and I have a rolodex of coffee spots throughout NBA cities.”

Kispert started posting social media videos from his visits to specialty shops, which caught the eye of Ike Bubna, a GU fan who operates three New Love Coffee shops in the Spokane area.

“That was kind of the precursor to starting The Bitter Truth,” Kispert said of the videos. “Ike cold called me, said if I was interested, he’d love to work with me.”

There was mutual interest. After sampling various roasts, The Bitter Truth launched with light, medium and dark roasts that are also available in decaf at BitterTruthCoffee.com. The beans are imported from Rwanda, Ethiopia, Peru and Guatemala, then roasted, packaged and shipped from New Love Coffee.

The Bitter Truth Website includes hats, coffee mugs and roasts in wholesale for businesses. Kispert was traded from Washington to Atlanta last January and the Hawks offer Bitter Truth coffee at the team facility. Kispert’s teammates with the Wizards and Hawks have been faithful customers and Jenn assists with design, marketing and messaging.

On typical game days, Kispert has two or three cups in the morning, an ice coffee following a pre-game nap, another cup upon arriving at the arena – “It’s usually cold in there so another coffee is great” – and a pre-game espresso shot.

“It’s really a different avenue to pour time and energy into when I’m not on the court,” said Kispert, who earned a business administration degree at GU and was halfway to an MBA. “In season, luckily, I have Ike and a few others helping me out. If we get into town for a road game, I’ll spend a couple hours working on it in the hotel room.”

Kispert’s name recognition, particularly in Spokane, Seattle, Washington D.C. and Atlanta, helps attract customers and he’s confident the product matches up well in the competitive coffee marketplace. Eleven former or current NFL players, including Kansas City quarterback Patrick Mahomes and Cooper Kupp, a former Eastern Washington standout who has won Super Bowls with the Los Angeles Rams and Seattle Seahawks, are in the coffee industry.

“The more people that try it, the more positive reviews I get,” Kispert said. “It’s differentiating myself and our company from thousands of others where you can get your coffee.”

“We got really good numbers on the launch, a lot of people came out to support it. As many businesses experience as you get into the 3- to 6-month mark, it sort of plateaus. We’re at a good level. This summer we’re beefing up and tuning up to get some growth so we can take on a bigger load when the season gets going.”

Gonzaga.title: 'You're all in wherever you're at': Corey Kispert talks Hawks, Few's Hall call and impact on his career
Gonzaga.summary:
Corey Kispert was one of the few constants during 4½ seasons with the Washington Wizards.

Teammates came and went, including former Zag Rui Hachimura. The coaching staff and front office changed. It added up to a lot of losses – a combined 33-131 in his last two full seasons after 35-47 records in each of his first two NBA seasons – and zero playoff appearances.

It was the polar opposite of his four seasons at Gonzaga. The Zags went 127-12 from 2018 to 2021 and made runs to the Sweet 16, Elite Eight and national championship game. The Zags were a shoo-in to be a No. 1 seed before the 2020 NCAA Tournament was canceled due to the COVID-19 pandemic. Kispert was a consensus first-team All-American in 2021.

When he was traded to Atlanta in January, Kispert landed in the middle of a playoff chase but also had to fit into a new system and new roster.

“It felt like a new experience for me,” Kispert said. “It had been so long since I played in a playoffs or tournament type situation. But compared to the other teams that played the (NBA champion Knicks), it was a really respectable effort against them (4-2 series loss in the opening round).

“It was really fun to relive and relearn super competitive, high level basketball.”

The 6-foot-6, 225-pound wing has proven to be a steady, reliable player, whether starting or coming off the bench in five NBA seasons. He averaged 9.2 points in 19 Wizards games and 9.2 points in 38 contests with Hawks following the trade.

Kispert averaged double figures in three seasons, including a career-best 13.4 points in 2023-24. He’s hit 38% of his career 3-pointers, 62.1% on 2s and 80.3% at the free-throw line.

“You’re all in wherever you’re at, especially when you’re young in the league,” said Kispert, selected 15th overall in the 2021 draft. “It’s keep playing and earn that next contract. The winner in you and competitor inside gets antsy and itchy. Washington did a lot for me and poured a lot into me. You kind of have to grow where you’re planted.”

Kispert’s time as a Zag and Wizard helped speed up his transition to being a Hawk.

“Sticking with it, just not giving up, being consistent, stacking days,” he said. “It was a grind my first couple years in Washington. The first two years we were trying to compete and push and it didn’t work out. We switched to a total rebuild halfway through, so I’ve seen it all in how organizations are trying to do it, how to build a team.

“The commitment to being a really good teammate and someone you like having around and being around has helped me more than I could have imagined. Washington allowed me some leeway to figure it out.”

The Hawks appear to be on the rise in the Eastern Conference, even though Philadelphia, Boston, Miami and the Knicks hogged the offseason headlines.

“I definitely feel like we’re a more complete team (going into the 2026-27 season),” Kispert said. “There’s a lot of buzz coming out of Philly, Miami, Boston and New York, but we definitely feel we can stand toe to toe.”

“The fit is really good. The main thing is I wish I had a full training camp and full season (with the Hawks). The chemistry you need to learn and the camaraderie you get during a full season – getting thrown in the middle of it is something everyone has to get used to. Coach (Quin) Snyder and I see the game the same way. We have a lot of younger, talented guys that are easy to get along with, so I’m excited for a full year and training camp.”

Kispert spends offseasons in Phoenix, usually getting in morning workouts and training sessions and playing pick-up games with numerous NBA players, including several of the hometown Suns. The Hawks also held workouts in Las Vegas and Los Angeles leading into the beginning of training camp in late September.

Kispert nailed nearly 44% of 385 3-point attempts in his last two seasons as a Zag. He buried 42.4% in his second season with the Wizards and was just under 40% last year when the trade to Atlanta was finalized.

“In order to take another step in my career, I have to be a truly elite shooter,” he said. “It’s all kinds of shots, off the dribble, open, contested, moving, especially from 3. I’ve been a very good shooter and I’ve been elite a couple of years. I need to put it together more consistently.

“And then just lean into and embrace my strength and physicality, especially on the defensive front. You have to be able to play both sides of the ball in the NBA. I’m not claiming to be a truly lockdown guy, but I need to lean into how strong I am and athletically I can make more of an impact.”

Kispert credited Gonzaga coach Mark Few’s impact on his career, even if the road was bumpy at times, particularly during his freshman and sophomore seasons.

“It took me a long time to realize what he’s doing, a long time to realize this guy is a Hall of Famer and he has a plan for me,” Kispert said. “Early on, the tough love was so jarring for me, that level of being on me was something I hadn’t experienced.

“But there were multiple moments where he said, ‘I wouldn’t be hard on someone that I didn’t believe in and didn’t believe had a future. Keep going, keep stacking days.’ ”

Kispert started all but one game in his last three seasons and his scoring averages soared from 8.0 to 13.9 to 18.6. His shooting percentages were off the charts as a senior: 62.8% on 2s, 44.0% on 3s and 87.8% at the foul line.

“If you’re mentally strong enough and believe in yourself enough, the other side, the amount of freedom and to have the keys was life-changing and career-changing for me when it fully clicked in,” Kispert said. “His feel for me as a person and how much he could push and ride me, was a huge credit. All of that was stuff I’ve leaned on in the NBA.

“I couldn’t be happier for him. No one could be more deserving of the Hall of Fame and I’m so happy all the work that it takes to build a program like that has culminated in such an awesome honor.”

Gonzaga.title: Gonzaga point guard commit Nathan De Sousa scheduled to arrive in Spokane next week; still awaiting NCAA eligibility
Gonzaga.summary:
Gonzaga’s point guard situation is still in flux less than three months out from the regular season, but help could be on the way as soon as next week.

Nathan De Sousa, a 23-year-old French point guard who spent the last five seasons playing professionally for Cholet Basket of the LNB Elite, is planning to arrive in Spokane next week, he told The Spokesman-Review on Saturday.

De Sousa, who committed to Gonzaga in June, is still waiting on the NCAA to process his eligibility waiver but is scheduled to fly to the United States as soon as he obtains a travel visa, which could happen in the upcoming days.

The Frenchman may be one solution for Gonzaga at the point guard spot after German prospect Jack Kayil kept his name in the NBA Draft and returning starter Mario Saint-Supery left the team in July to sign a long-term professional contract with Spanish club Valencia.

Mark Few’s program recently picked up a commitment from 5-in-5 Dayton transfer Javon Bennett, but the point guard’s future at Gonzaga is now uncertain after the NCAA was granted a stay motion in the Ohio injunction that previously granted him a fifth year of eligibility.

Meanwhile, De Sousa, fellow Gonzaga commit Izan Almansa and dozens of international players currently committed to Division I programs continue to wait on the NCAA to approve eligibility waivers, with roughly a week until the fall semester starts and preseason practices begin at most schools.

If cleared, the 6-3 De Sousa would give Gonzaga an experienced playmaker and serviceable shooter at one of the most important positions in Few’s offense. A native of Saint-Quentin, France, the guard averaged 10.9 points, 4.9 rebounds, 2.5 assists and 1.9 turnovers last season for Cholet in LNB Elite play.

De Sousa made 43.4% of his shots from the field and connected at 36.1% from the 3-point line, up from 18.8% the season prior. He also shot 76.9% at the free-throw line. Playing in Cholet’s backcourt alongside Gerald Ayayi, the younger brother of former GU guard Joel Ayayi, De Sousa averaged another 8.3 ppg, 4.7 apg and 2.0 rpg in the Basketball Champions League, shooting 31.7% from the field, 28.6% from the 3-point line and 84.4% from the free-throw line.

Cholet advanced to the semifinal round of the LNB Elite playoffs before losing in a four-game series to Paris Basketball. De Sousa averaged 7.7 ppg and 3.2 apg during the French playoffs.

The guard has competed for Cholet’s senior team four of the last five seasons, leaving in 2022-23 to play for AS Alsace in France’s second professional division. De Sousa started in Cholet’s youth academy in 2018 and played two seasons with the club’s U-21 team before being promoted to the senior team.

Gonzaga.title: Gonzaga point guard commit Javon Bennett encounters eligibility setback after NCAA stay granted in Ohio case
Gonzaga.summary:
The ongoing, often-unpredictable NCAA 5-in-5 saga has thrown another wrench into the plans of Gonzaga point guard commit Javon Bennett.

A Dayton transfer who committed to Gonzaga on Aug. 5, Bennett encountered a setback on Friday when the NCAA was granted a stay motion in the federal NCAA v. Wisne lawsuit that protected the point guard and all other student-athletes hoping to secure a fifth year of eligibility.

It’s the second decision in the last five days that could impact whether Bennett is able to suit up for a Gonzaga team that still doesn’t have a point guard signed to its 2026-27 roster.

On Monday, the NCAA notched another legal victory when the Ohio Court of Appeals granted a motion to stay an injunction in the Borovicanin v. NCAA lawsuit that included Bennett and 14 other athletes. The Court of Appeals set oral arguments for Sept. 22, suggesting there could be a decision in the Ohio case before Gonzaga opens the college basketball season on Nov. 2.

For now, both of the injunctions that allowed Bennett to pursue a fifth season of eligibility – the federal one in Colorado and state injunction in Ohio – will be on hold until appeals in both cases are resolved. The point guard was scheduled to arrive in Spokane this Thursday, he recently told The Spokesman-Review in a phone interview.

“Effective immediately, the age-based eligibility rules will be implemented as the Division I membership intended,” the NCAA wrote in a statement delivered to member schools Friday. “Class members who were allowed to compete because of the Wisne injunction are no longer eligible to compete.

“The Association will separately continue to defend other similar putative class action lawsuits and the state court cases that have been filed by former student-athletes seeking additional eligibility and expeditiously appeal any cases where former student-athletes have, or will, be granted additional eligibility through separate state court rulings. We are encouraged by the Ohio Court of Appeals’ decision to stay the first of those injunctions pending our appeal.”

A handful of other players involved in various state lawsuits, including Gonzaga commit Chauncey Wiggins – a fifth-year wing from Florida State who earned an injunction in his home state of Georgia – still have a clear path to eligibility for the time being. Wiggins arrived in Spokane on Friday, according to a photo posted to his Instagram story from McCarthey Athletic Center.

Gonzaga has also been linked to multiple point guard prospects recently named in a similar California lawsuit, including Florida’s Xaivian Lee. On Tuesday, the 73 athletes named in the California suit were granted a temporary restraining order against the NCAA, enabling that group to pursue a fifth season of eligibility.

The NCAA is expected to file for stay motions in other state lawsuits, but it hasn’t had a 100% success rate. A court in Tennessee recently rejected the NCAA’s motion to stay an injunction that extended the eligibility for 19 player plaintiffs.

Gonzaga.title: Gonzaga guard Adam Miller signs professional contract with Belgian club Oostende
Gonzaga.summary:
On the heels of a lengthy college basketball career that culminated with a brief stop at Gonzaga, Adam Miller has signed a contract with Basketball Club Coretec Oostende in Belgium’s top professional league.

The shooting guard agreed to one-year contract with Corotec Oostende, according to a news release from the club Thursday. The team competes in the city of Oostende, a suburb of Bruges located on the northwestern coast of the country.

Miller played five college seasons over five years, transferring last summer to Gonzaga, where he started in 25 of 35 games and averaged 7.3 points and 1.6 rebounds.

The 6-foot-3 guard was brought to Spokane as a quality perimeter threat who could enhance the team’s outside shooting, but generally struggled from 3-point range, making just 30.2% of his shots after connecting at a 42.9% clip the year prior.

Miller was in and out of Gonzaga’s starting lineup, coming off the bench in the team’s opener against Texas Southern before starting in the next seven games and eventually sliding back into a reserve role. The guard moved back into the first five ahead of a Jan. 8 game against Santa Clara and started in the final 18 games.

Miller reached double figures in 11 games and scored a season-high 21 points, making 7 of 8 shots from the free throw line, in a key road win at Santa Clara on Feb. 14.

Gonzaga was the fourth and final stop for Miller, a former top-40 national recruit who played on Team USA’s FIBA U-18 World Cup gold medal-winning team with ex-Zag Chet Holmgren.

The Peoria, Illinois, native played one season at Illinois in 2020-21, teaming up with former Illini and current Gonzaga assistant Stephen Gentry, before using a medical redshirt in 2021-22 and transferring to LSU for the 2022-23 season. Miller started in all 33 games for the Tigers before transferring to Arizona State for the 2023-24 and 2024-25 seasons, starting in 51 of the 53 games he played for Bobby Hurley’s Sun Devils.

Haaland lands in Spain

Former Gonzaga walk-on Noah Haaland, a native of Rathdrum, is starting his professional career in Spain’s second division.

Haaland signed a contract with Hestia Menorca, a Primera FEB club located on the Spanish Balearic island of Menorca.

The 24-year-old forward played in 13 games over two seasons at Gonzaga, briefly entering the team’s frontcourt rotation in 2025-26 when starters Graham Ike and Braden Huff were both sidelined with injuries.

Haaland averaged 2.0 points and 1.1 rebounds in 10 appearances last season, making his lone start on Senior Day against Portland on Feb. 25. Haaland scored a career-high 10 points with four rebounds in 11 minutes against Pepperdine on Jan. 21, going 4 of 4 from the field and 2 of 2 from the free throw line.

The 6-foot-9 forward played two seasons at Allan Hancock College in California before transferring to Gonzaga in 2024. At Lakeland High, he earned All-4A Inland Empire League honors as a junior and senior, helping the Hawks advance to the 4A state tournament in 2021.

Haaland’s father, Dale, played two seasons at Gonzaga from 1985-87 and his mother, Robyn Benson, is a former Zags volleyball player.

Gonzaga.title: Ivy League opponent Cornell visiting Gonzaga for New Year's Eve nonconference matchup
Gonzaga.summary:
Gonzaga will face an Ivy League opponent on New Year’s Eve before turning the page on its nonconference schedule and diving into Pac-12 Conference play.

Mark Few’s program will host Cornell on Dec. 31, according to a report on Friday from Bracketeer.com’s Rocco Miller. A tipoff time and television details will be announced at a later date.

The New Year’s Eve matchup technically won’t mark the end of GU’s nonconference schedule – the Zags will travel to Detroit on Feb. 20 to play Duke – but is expected to be the final nonleague game before Few’s team opens Pac-12 play in January.

The Cornell matchup becomes the fourth known home nonconference game for Gonzaga, which will also host New Mexico State (Nov. 7), Montana State (Nov. 17) and NAIA Eastern Oregon (Dec. 2). LSU is also visiting Spokane for a Nov. 14 matchup at Numerica Veterans Arena.

This will be the first-ever meeting between Gonzaga and Cornell and signifies just the second matchup between the Zags and an opponent from the Ivy League. Yale visited Spokane on two occasions, traveling to Numerica Veterans Arena in 1992 before returning to play at McCarthey Athletic Center in 2023.

Cornell placed fourth in the Ivy League standings last season, finishing with an overall record of 15-13 and conference mark of 8-6.

Third-year coach Jon Jaques, a former Cornell captain from 2006-10, is replacing each of his three double-digit scorers from a year ago, including guards Cooper Noard (18.2 points per game) and Jake Fiegen (17.1 ppg). The team’s top returner is starting point guard Jacob Beccles, who averaged 7.7 points, 3.1 assists and 2.5 rebounds.

Gonzaga’s nonconference schedule still hasn’t been finalized, but as of now the Cornell matchup is the team’s only game between a Dec. 19 showdown with Michigan State in Palm Springs and the end of the calendar year.

Gonzaga.title: How Gonzaga's offseason evolved into a roster-building roller coaster: 'Like nothing we've ever seen'
Gonzaga.summary:
The catalogue of words Mark Few could use to describe Gonzaga’s offseason is too long to run through, but the newly enshrined Hall of Fame coach landed on some appropriate terms during a breakdown of the five-ish months that have elapsed since his team exited the NCAA Tournament with a Round of 32 loss to Texas.

First, there was “frustrating,” followed by “not usual” and finally “crazy.”

“Like nothing we’ve ever seen and it’s been frustrating, but it’s just different in this day and age,” Few said last weekend during a media session at Mohegan Sun Casino in Uncasville, Connecticut, one day before he was enshrined into the Naismith Hall of Fame. “It’s been not usual, but like we just got done talking about, you have to adapt.”

“Turbulent” might be another term to characterize the roster-building roller coaster Few and his coaching staff have navigated since the early stages of April.

Just 44 days out from Kraziness in the Kennel, Gonzaga has eight scholarship players officially signed to its 2026-27 roster with two more walk-ons. In other words, if the Zags held their annual Kraziness showcase tomorrow, they’d have exactly the number of bodies required to run through a traditional 5-on-5 intrasquad scrimmage, but no more than that.

A full roster is still expected the time Gonzaga opens the season on Nov. 2 against Purdue for a potential top-25 showdown in Las Vegas, but it could hinge on a number of things well outside of Few’s control – something that’s become a primary source of angst for the new Hall of Famer and coaching peers around the country the last handful of months as they try to finalize their teams before the fall semester starts.

The issues Gonzaga faces now are partially a byproduct of unforeseen developments that came earlier in the offseason. When former signee Jack Kayil unexpectedly kept his name in the NBA Draft on May 13, most quality transfer portal options at his position had already committed to play elsewhere, limiting Gonzaga’s replacement options. (Kayil was selected No. 39 overall by the New York Knicks, but the combo guard will be stashed in Europe after signing a five-year extension with German club Alba Berlin).

The transfer portal was bone-dry when starting point guard Mario Saint-Supery abruptly left Gonzaga’s program, catching fans and Few’s coaching staff completely off guard on July 11 when he signed a four-year, seven-figure contract with Spanish ACB club Valencia.

Gonzaga had a contingency plan in place, but even that has come with complications.

On June 26, the Zags landed a commitment from French guard Nathan De Sousa, a 23-year-old professional who’s spent the last five seasons with Cholet of LNB Elite. De Sousa would’ve been a top-notch backup to Saint-Supery and could prove to be more than serviceable as a starter in the new Pac-12 Conference, but both he and Gonzaga forward commit Izan Almansa – a 6-foot-10 forward who played last season at Real Madrid – are still waiting on the NCAA to approve eligibility waivers.

In an attempt to prohibit highly compensated European pros from entering college basketball, the sport’s governing body indicated earlier this summer it would not clear any player who was paid above “actual and necessary expenses.”

“We’ve had several of the European kids that the NCAA’s kind of acted like they’re going to change how they interpret these and they didn’t even do it midstream, they did it when you’re already through your recruiting cycle, which has just been crazy,” Few said. “We voiced our concerns, all of us coaches have to them. We don’t know what’s going to happen with how they rule Europeans, even though they were letting everyone in last year. Now the five-year thing has happened…”

Ah yes, the five-year thing.

Gonzaga’s second contingency plan has transformed into a late-summer headache for coaches and players around the country. It stems from the NCAA’s decision in late June to adopt age-based eligibility rules, allowing athletes to play five seasons over five years.

The new rules weren’t intended to grandfather in seniors who completed their eligibility in 2025-26, but the NCAA’s timing gave a large crowd of fifth-year hopefuls a long enough runway to challenge the regulatory body in court with hopes of securing another season.

“Listen, I think if the courts are going to rule them eligible and they’re eligible, I don’t know why anybody would ever say anything about them,” Few said. “I think many people have spoke about how that particular class is the only one that hasn’t had this. Moving forward they’re going to have it and behind them was COVID. It’s one class so you’re like, ‘yeah they’re right.’ ”

Now, less than two months out from preseason exhibition games, programs like Gonzaga have made late-summer additions fill holes at certain positions and generally erase any lingering uncertainty around their rosters.

The result? More uncertainty.

Gonzaga picked up two quick commitments, one from 5-10 Dayton point guard Javon Bennett, who was ruled eligible after prevailing in an Ohio lawsuit, and another from 6-10 Florida State wing Chauncey Wiggins, who won a similar case in his home state of Georgia.

Neither have signed financial aid agreements with Gonzaga, and there’s some apprehension around Bennett’s situation after the NCAA was granted a motion to stay the Ohio case on Monday, potentially reversing the guard’s eligibility. Bennett is still protected by the federal Wisne vs. NCAA injunction approved earlier this month in Colorado, but the guard could encounter another hurdle if the NCAA is also granted a stay in that case.

“It’s definitely a crazy time in college basketball,” Bennett said. “For me, when I heard I was left out of that 5-in-5 window, I was definitely devastated. I think if you’re going to give players after us a chance, I don’t see why we wouldn’t be able to get a chance. I think it’s fair for us to appeal to that situation and like I said, I think kids that have somewhere to play will be able to benefit from the 5-in-5.”

Wiggins, who could figure into Gonzaga’s starting lineup at the small forward spot after averaging 13.3 pints and making 38.7% of his 3-pointers last season, is on solid ground for the time being as someone protected by both the Georgia and Colorado federal lawsuits.

“I do think the NCAA should’ve grandfathered us in,” Wiggins said. “The way I see it is, when my class got into college we played against fifth-year and sixth-years. Then when we’re about to leave college, you’re telling me you’re going to give everybody after us five years. And some of us, I think like me still fit that age. The age requirement they were talking about, I fit that. Some of us in the 2022 class fit that, so I think the NCAA personally should’ve gave us another year.

“College sports is college sports, it’s got some chaos right now. I do think they will appeal – I don’t really know, but I think they might appeal the Colorado one because that was for everybody and it came out of the blue.”

Coaches who’ve already finalized their rosters, or refuse to dip into the 5-in-5 pool out of principle, have been critical of peers relying on fifth-year players to improve their teams.

“At some point, you’ve got to care about the sport,” UConn’s Dan Hurley said. “Especially if the sport has given you a lot. Doing things to hurt the sport so that you can win a little bit more, you’ve got to look in the mirror a little on that.”

Few, who’s been on numerous coaching and college basketball committees throughout his 28-year tenure at Gonzaga, was one of the coaches imploring the NCAA to wait on announcing new 5-in-5 eligibility rules, anticipating the chaos that’s ensued over the last two months.

“Behind the scenes, some of us coaches told the NCAA over and over again,” Few said. “If they waited longer to announce this, they probably wouldn’t have this issue. So I don’t know why anybody would not be open to it. Maybe you don’t need it, but if you do … these are good guys. The kids we’re recruiting graduated from college, they’re going to our grad school and they’re great people, great assets to our program. I don’t know why you wouldn’t do that.”

In this fluid college basketball climate, it could be a matter of days, weeks or months until Gonzaga is able to call its roster complete. It’s not unfamiliar territory for a program that waited on a judge’s decision at the 11th hour last season to learn if transfer wing Tyon Grant-Foster would be eligible to play.

The Zags ostensibly received positive news on Thursday, when Real Madrid penned a farewell letter to Almansa, suggesting the forward is one step closer to making it official with Few’s program.

For now, a frustrating, crazy and unusual Gonzaga offseason will bleed into the final days of August.

Gonzaga.title: Montana State program coming off strong Big Sky season set to visit Gonzaga on Nov. 17
Gonzaga.summary:
Gonzaga hasn’t released its final nonconference schedule, but anyone willing to do some digging can probably discover a few of the missing pieces.

For example, a quick internet search of Montana State’s schedule would’ve led someone to the third known home game of Gonzaga’s 2026-27 nonleague slate.

According to Montana State’s athletics website, the Bobcats are scheduled to visit Gonzaga on Nov. 17, one week before Mark Few’s program takes on the 16-team Players Era Festival in Las Vegas.

A tipoff time and television broadcast details will be announced at a later date.

SB Nation’s Gonzaga website, Slipper Still Fits, identified the matchup with Montana State hours after The Spokesman-Review discovered another home game against NAIA Eastern Oregon, thanks to an updated schedule on the Mountaineers’ site.

With the additions of Montana State and Eastern Oregon, the Zags now have 12 known dates on their nonconference schedule, not including a potential championship matchup at the Players Era event on Nov. 28. Gonzaga will play at least four nonleague games in Spokane and won’t have to leave town between a Nov. 2 opener against Purdue at T-Mobile Arena in Vegas and the team’s return to Sin City on Nov. 24 for Players Era.

There have been 49 previous meetings between Gonzaga and Montana State, but none since 1997, with a majority of the prior matchups occurring while both programs were part of the Big Sky Conference. The Zags have a 27-22 advantage in the all-time series and have prevailed in seven of the last nine meetings.

Under the guidance of fourth-year coach Matt Logie, who earned a four-year contract extension on Wednesday, the Bobcats have won exactly 50% of their games, going 18-14 last season, 15-18 in 2024-25 and 17-18 in 2023-24 for a total record of 50-50. Montana State earned an automatic NCAA Tournament berth during Logie’s first season, marking the program’s third straight trip to March Madness. The Bobcats went each of the two previous years under former coach Danny Sprinkle, who’s now at Washington.

Montana State loses its top three scorers from a team that finished second in the Big Sky with a 12-6 record before losing to Idaho in the second round of the conference tournament.

The Bobcats have to replace more than 31 points per game from their starting lineup, but they do return their fourth, fifth and sixth-leading scorers, including forward Christian King, a Kirkland native and Seattle Prep graduate who averaged 12.6 points and 4.5 rebounds last season.

Gonzaga.title: Gonzaga scheduled to host familiar NAIA opponent for nonconference game on Dec. 2
Gonzaga.summary:
Another home date has been added to Gonzaga’s nonconference calendar.

Eastern Oregon, an NAIA program that has frequented McCarthey Athletic Center over the years, is returning to Spokane for a nonleague game on Dec. 2, according to the Mountaineers’ schedule.

The matchup will figure into Gonzaga’s overall record but count as an exhibition for Eastern Oregon, which competes in the Cascade Collegiate Conference. It becomes the second known home game on the Zags’ nonconference schedule and third known game in Spokane, joining the Nov. 7 home opener against New Mexico State and Nov. 14 matchup against LSU at Numerica Veterans Arena.

The Mountaineers have made three recent trips to the Kennel under sixth-year coach Matt Kemp, visiting on Oct. 31, 2021, for a matchup that counted as an exhibition for both teams. The Zags had six players reach double figures en route to a 115-62 victory.

Each of Eastern Oregon’s last two visits were exhibition contests for the Mountaineers that factored into Gonzaga’s regular-season schedule. That included a 120-42 victory for Gonzaga on Dec. 28, 2022, that signified the largest margin of victory in program history. Drew Timme led seven double-digit scorers with 18 points in 18 minutes.

Gonzaga cleared the century mark for the third time in as many meetings the next season, winning 123-57 on Nov. 14, 2023. Graham Ike was one of three 20-point scorers for GU, leading the game with 25 points and 11 rebounds in just 18 minutes. Braden Huff, the only player from that game who will suit up against EOU this fall, had 23 points for the Zags.

Second-year Gonzaga graduate assistant Que Johnson was on Kemp’s staff at EOU as a top assistant coach for each of the last three meetings between the schools. There are a pair of connections to the Inland Northwest on the Mountaineers’ 2026-27 roster, including former Coeur d’Alene High standout Logan Orchard and Caleb Schroeder, a Post Falls native who played at Genesis Prep.

The Dec. 2 game will either come four or five days after GU’s finishes up at the Players Era in Las Vegas. The Zags will either close the 16-team tournament on Nov. 27 or 28, depending on if they qualify for the championship game.

Three days after the EOU matchup, Gonzaga will travel to play UCLA in a neutral-site, nonconference game at the Honda Center in Anaheim, California.

Gonzaga.summary: ANAHEIM, Calif. (Aug. 18, 2026) – Official fan travel packages for the West Coast Hoops Showdown featuring UCLA and Gonzaga are on sale now, providing fans with an opportunity to secure their tickets and accommodations for one of the marquee matchups of the 2026-27 college basketball season.

Gonzaga.title: Former Gonzaga guard Malachi Smith inks contract with Toronto Raptors
Gonzaga.summary:
Four months after closing the 2025-26 NBA season against the Toronto Raptors, former Gonzaga guard Malachi Smith has signed a contract with the Eastern Conference franchise.

Per NBA rules, the terms of Smith’s deal were not disclosed by the organization.

Smith made his NBA debut last season with the Brooklyn Nets and played 15 games with the team in March and April, signing consecutive 10-day contracts before agreeing to a non-guaranteed deal to close out the regular season.

The guard became a free agent on July 10 when he was waived by Brooklyn and did not sign with a team to play NBA Summer League in Las Vegas.

Smith was productive and efficient in the limited minutes he played for Brooklyn last year, averaging 8.3 points, 3.4 rebounds and 3.3 assists on 48.5% shooting and 43.5% from the 3-point line.

He reached double figures in seven of his 15 games and wasn’t far off from a triple-double while scoring 19 points with 10 assists and eight rebounds on April 10 against the Milwaukee Bucks.

Smith saw an uptick in playing time near the end of the season, logging at least 36 minutes in each of his last four games, including 40 minutes against the Indiana Pacers and 43 against the Bucks. He closed the season with eight points, six assists and five rebounds against the Toronto team he signed with Monday.

Before a monthlong stint with the Nets, Smith played for Brooklyn’s G League affiliate in Long Island. Prior to that, the former Zag spent two seasons playing for three G League teams: the Rip City Remix (Portland Trail Blazers), Wisconsin Herd (Milwaukee Bucks) and Memphis Hustle (Memphis Grizzlies).

Smith spent one season at Gonzaga in 2022-23 after playing two seasons at Chattanooga and one at Wright State. He earned West Coast Conference Sixth Man of the Year honors after averaging 8.7 points, 3.6 rebounds and 1.4 assists while making 53.6% of his shots from the field and shooting an impressive 50% from the 3-point line.

Gonzaga.title: Few Enshrined into Naismith Basketball Hall of Fame
Gonzaga.summary: SPRINGFIELD, Mass. – Flanked by three men who represented different facets of his journey, Gonzaga men's basketball coach Mark Few officially joined the game's legends Saturday night, becoming a member of the 2026 class inducted into the Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame.

Gonzaga.title: 'What are the chances?' Gonzaga legend John Stockton proud to have company from alma mater in Naismith HOF | Notebook
Gonzaga.summary:
SPRINGFIELD, Mass. – Fifteen years before Gonzaga transformed into an undisputed college basketball power, the small Jesuit university in Spokane made a brief flicker on the national stage with a standout point guard from a high school just down the street.

Gonzaga Prep’s John Stockton captured WCAC Player of the Year in 1984, earned all-conference honors in consecutive seasons and was selected 16th overall by the Utah Jazz in the 1984 NBA draft. Chances are you know the rest of the story.

Stockton’s Naismith Hall of Fame induction call came in 2009, six years after the NBA’s all-time assists leader wrapped up a distinguished, record-setting career with the Utah Jazz and 25 years removed from his final game in a Zag uniform.

But would the point guard ever have company in Springfield, Massachusetts? The odds of another Gonzaga induction always seemed low. Lightning usually doesn’t strike twice for a midmajor school in a small-market city like Spokane, but Stockton was always willing to make room if somebody else ever came along.

“It’s unbelievable and special. What are the chances?” Stockton said Friday, 24 hours before Gonzaga coach Mark Few officially joined him in the pantheon of college and professional basketball as a newly enshrined Hall of Famer. “You look back 30, maybe 40 years ago and you would’ve never thought any of this could happen. So it’s pretty exciting for all of us.”

Stockton isn’t the only one who would’ve found it hard to believe that Gonzaga – and by extension Spokane – would have multiple representatives in the Hall of Fame, considering how the program’s trajectory looked in the late 1980s and early 1990s before Dan Fitzgerald, Dan Monson and eventually Few launched an unprecedented run over the next three decades.

Before Gonzaga coaches could pitch potential recruits on joining a program that routinely won conference championships, made deep NCAA Tournament runs and sent players into the NBA on a nearly annual basis, they had just one legitimate selling point: a homegrown point guard who bucked the odds to become the first player from Gonzaga taken in the first round of the NBA draft.

“He was the only one anyone could ever talk about the first 15 years on the recruiting trail, or 10 years,” Few said of Stockton.

Stockton still resides in Spokane and maintains a close relationship with Gonzaga’s longtime coach, hosting dozens of Few’s active and former players for offseason 5-on-5 runs at his Warehouse facility a few hundred feet from McCarthey Athletic Center.

“It’s super special,” Few said of joining Stockton in the Hall of Fame. “He and I are great friends and I just couldn’t have more respect for a human being than I do for him and how he’s lived his life and been such a great example and been such a great torch-bearer for Gonzaga.”

As part of the enshrinement ceremony, members of the 2026 class were able to select presenters to join them on stage in Springfield. The only stipulation was that presenters must already be in the Hall themselves. Few started with a phone call to another 509 number.

“Obviously the first one I thought of was John,” Gonzaga’s coach said.

Stockton’s second-youngest son, David, was 18 years old when he traveled to Springfield in 2009 for his father’s enshrinement. A former Gonzaga walk-on who climbed the ladder to earn starting minutes for Few’s Sweet 16 team in 2013-14 before setting out on a professional career, David was among the group of former players that traveled to the East Coast to attend Hall of Fame festivities on Friday and Saturday.

“It’s so hard to imagine this happening from a small town like Spokane and Gonzaga the school,” David said. “Coach Few is what’s right with basketball. Sticking around when most coaches would leave and you just don’t see it anymore.

“He was hard on me and as a walk-on, they treated us like they should’ve and they helped me become a better player and I’ll always credit my ability to play any sort of professional game to my years with him, so I appreciate it.”

Respect from coach to coach

Few’s unrivaled accomplishments at Gonzaga have garnered deep respect from coaches at every level, including both of the NBA pioneers that joined him in the Hall of Fame’s 2026 class.

In total, there are 2,836 career victories between the three coaches honored at Saturday’s enshrinement ceremony. Few accounts for 773 of those with Mike D’Antoni adding another 1,199 and Doc Rivers leading the group with a whopping 2,060 wins.

Rivers, best known for his nine-year run with the Boston Celtics, which included an NBA title in 2007-08, has admired Few’s work afar and acknowledged the difficulty of reaching college basketball’s mountaintop from a midmajor program like Gonzaga.

“Amazing,” Rivers said Friday during a media session at Mohegan Sun Casino in Uncasville, Connecticut. “To me he’s an innovator because he did it at a place – with us growing up, you had to be at UCLA, you had to be at these certain locations to build a winner one time. He keeps doing it over and over and over and over again. Every year he has a chance to win a national title. It goes back to what I was saying. People think winning it is easy and it’s not.

“Everything has to go right and it has to go right for him one day. That doesn’t diminish anything he’s done. He’s changed college sports in a lot of ways because he proved the small market schools can be successful continually.”

D’Antoni, who had five coaching stints in the NBA and introduced the vaunted “seven seconds or less” offense, doesn’t monitor college basketball during the regular season but can count on catching Few and the Zags every year in the NCAA Tournament.

“I know he’s an unbelievable coach at a great program from kind of a midmajor school, not like a Kentucky or whatever,” D’Antoni said. “He’s taken it to heights that are incredible. I don’t follow college basketball that much, but I do tune in when they’re rolling in the tournament. I love the way they play and their style and obviously to get him here, he’s a great coach.”

On display in Springfield

By Saturday afternoon, the Naismith Hall of Fame museum had already completed personalized display cases for each of its 2026 inductees.

Few and family members toured the newly finished “Hall of Honor” exhibit on Saturday afternoon, a handful of hours before they strolled down a red carpet into Symphony Hall for the evening’s enshrinement ceremony.

The glass case commemorating Few included mementos from his career and possibly the most fitting symbol of his life away from the court : a used fly-fishing rod the coach donated to the downtown Springfield museum. The exhibit also included a fly-fishing photo, a Gonzaga NCAA Tournament ring, a Team USA pullover and a photo of Few with LeBron James from the 2024 Paris Olympics.

Inside an adjacent room at the museum, visitors could scroll through a virtual, touchscreen slideshow detailing Few’s coaching timeline and depicting different images from his 28 years at Gonzaga and run with USA Basketball.

Few and other 2026 inductees each donated keepsakes to another display case in Springfield. The Gonzaga coach’s selection included his 2021 Naismith Coach of the Year trophy, a game-used basketball from his 700th career victory at Pepperdine on Jan. 18, 2024, and a poster from the program’s first Final Four appearance in 2017.

Gonzaga.title: Gonzaga's Mark Few filled with gratitude during Hall of Fame enshrinement: 'Couldn't even think about dreaming such a thing'
Gonzaga.summary:
SPRINGFIELD, Mass. – Mark Few’s long-shot journey to the Naismith Memorial Hall of Fame began with rejection, of all things.

As he delivered a Hall of Fame acceptance speech Saturday in front of a Symphony Hall audience that easily outnumbered the population of Few’s hometown in central Oregon, the Gonzaga coach went deep into his adolescent archives.

He traced back to a painful memory, but an important one.

A college-aged Few was applying to be the head basketball coach at his alma mater, Creswell High School. Few had a leg up on the competition, or so he thought, as a top Creswell assistant whose father, a town minister, played cards with the school superintendent, and mother worked locally as a nurse.

“Kind of seemed like I was a shoo-in,” Few said. “Well, I got shot down and here I am. So go figure.”

Springfield never felt too far away for the longtime Gonzaga coach. After all, it was situated just 10 miles north of his hometown, a 15-minute ride up Interstate 5. But enough about Springfield, Oregon.

Few could only come up with one explanation for how someone with his modest beginnings, raised in a town of 1,500, could reach this Springfield – the one located in southern Massachusetts, where millions of visitors travel to tour the iconic hoops shrine minutes from Symphony Hall and where on Saturday, college basketball’s active leader in winning percentage joined an esteemed group of inductees for the 2026 enshrinement ceremony.

Few surmises a greater power must have been at work.

“How else does a guy get from Creswell, Oregon, to Springfield, Massachusetts? Come on now, wow,” Few said. “The only Springfield I ever thought about was Springfield, Oregon, 10 miles north of Creswell. Looking around this room tonight, it’s so humbling to realize how many people shaped this journey. I may be the one standing here, but this honor belongs to so many others.”

During an acceptance speech that timed out at 13 minutes, Few considered the far-fetched scenarios that helped make his Hall of Fame career – one that will be difficult to replicate at the NCAA level – possible in the first place.

He showered family members, coaching colleagues and players with thank yous and gratitude, giving a special ode to Gonzaga predecessor Dan Monson, the man largely responsible for hooking Few up with a low-paying graduate assistant gig in Spokane before the 1989-90 season.

“I want to not only acknowledge but thank Dan Monson for not only giving me my start in coaching but more importantly, allowing me to stay rent-free in his apartment for two years at Gonzaga,” Few said. “My first salary was a whopping $1,500.”

The star-studded crowd that sat in on Few’s speech included Hall of Fame players Steve Nash, Tracy McGrady, Kevin Garnett, Ray Allen, Paul Pierce and Allen Iverson, college coaching luminaries Roy Williams and Jim Boeheim and celebrity attendees like Larry David. Cleveland Cavaliers guard James Harden reacted in astonishment when Few revealed his GA coaching salary.

Few introduced his trio of presenters, selected carefully by the Gonzaga coach to symbolize three different facets of his career. Seated by him on the stage were legendary Gonzaga/Utah Jazz guard John Stockton, Hall of Fame college coach John Calipari and NBA legend Grant Hill, who developed a relationship with Few through years of trips and experiences with USA Basketball.

“How about this All-Star class here, man?” Few said, pointing toward his presenters. “Stocks represents my Gonzaga time. His loyalty, his hard work, his values and how he always, always walks the talk. My main man Cal, for a friendship that started because nobody wanted to play us and we couldn’t get a game against the quote unquote blue bloods, so we started our own series and that worked out pretty dang good for us. … Finally Grant Hill, what a dude, man. … I’ll never, ever, ever forget the day he called and asked me to join the 2024 Olympic coaching staff. Grant, you’re an unbelievable leader and an even better friend.”

Most of Few’s immediate family members traveled to join the coach in Springfield, including wife Marcy, sons AJ, Joe and Colt, and daughter Julia. Few’s mother Barbara died in November 2025 at the age of 92 and his father, Norm, a longtime minister, was unable to travel to the ceremony from his home in Creswell.

“People often ask why I stuck around at Gonzaga for so long,” Few said. “My dad is 95 years old and probably currently struggling with the remote to find NBATV. But he was the pastor at the same little church in Creswell, Oregon, for 54 years, which has got to be a record.”

Few knows a thing or two about records. His coaching career is cloaked in them. Over 28 seasons, his Gonzaga teams have never failed to qualify for an NCAA Tournament. Sprinkled in were 14 trips to the Sweet 16, six Elite Eights and two national championship game appearances.

In hindsight, Few understands the body of work probably wouldn’t have been possible had he jumped for one of the countless power conference job offers that came his way through the years.

“(My dad) taught me that sometimes the greatest calling isn’t finding the next thing. It’s pouring everything you have into where you are,” Few said. “That’s what I learned from him, hence I stayed.”

Few’s pipeline of All-American and NBA players was well-represented Saturday, with everyone from multi-time NBA All-Star Domantas Sabonis to Gonzaga career scoring leader Drew Timme to 1999 Elite Eight hero Casey Calvary in attendance. Countless examples of the coaching tree Few has established were also in the crowd, including Arizona’s Tommy Lloyd, Gonzaga coach-in-waiting Brian Michaelson, Boise State’s Leon Rice and Valparaiso’s Roger Powell, to name a handful.

“This isn’t about me tonight,” Few said. “The greatest thing we built at Gonzaga wasn’t a basketball program. It was a family and a culture. It kept people wanting to come back. That is one of the greatest rewards that a coach who has stayed at the same place his whole career gets to experience.”

Former guard Matt Santangelo, a three-time All-WCC selection who played on the school’s 1999 Cinderella team, said this weekend’s enshrinement ceremony was “never on the bingo card” for a school of Gonzaga’s stature.

“It’s so hard to put into words and so many people have tried to capture what’s been accomplished and what’s been built at Gonzaga, but I don’t know if anyone’s ever really done it because it’s so foreign, so unusual, so rare,” Santangelo said. “Then the superlatives that go along with it. It is the greatest story in college sports. Here’s a guy who stayed loyal to his values and his character and said, why not here, why not us? Then went out and did it.”

Some of what Few did? Twenty-eight straight NCAA Tournament bids and counting. Seven-hundred seventy-three wins. Twenty-three regular-season conference championships. A career winning percentage of .832.

Not a bad career for someone who didn’t exactly nail his first job interview.

“What a crazy, crazy, surreal moment for me,” Few said. “… The town I grew up in had a population of 1,500 people. It had one stoplight. So to be standing where I am today is absolutely mind-boggling. I say that because people have asked me if this is a dream come true and I’m telling you, I couldn’t even think about dreaming such a thing where I came from.”

Gonzaga.title: How to Watch Naismith Hall of Fame Enshrinement Weekend
Gonzaga.summary: SPOKANE, Wash. – Gonzaga fans can watch head coach Mark Few take his place among basketball's legends this weekend when the Naismith Basketball Hall of Fame welcomes its Class of 2026 in Springfield, Mass.

Gonzaga.title: 'I felt my heart drop to my knees.' Ahead of Naismith enshrinement, Gonzaga's Mark Few flashes back to unique hall call
Gonzaga.summary:
UNCASVILLE, Conn. – Most of Mark Few’s favorite fly-fishing spots are tucked away in remote parts of Eastern Washington and Northern Idaho, where ponderosa pine trees vastly outnumber cell phone towers.

Generally speaking, the further from civilization the better.

It’s ideal when you’re looking to unplug and disconnect – not as much when you’re anticipating the type of phone call that comes once in a lifetime.

Few had reason to think one of those might be coming on March 31. He and an angling partner were miles out of town, just a minute or two from the river where they’d be casting their fly lines. Few’s cell signal probably wasn’t for long, but right as he prepared to enter a dead zone, the coach felt his phone vibrate.

The Naismith Basketball Hall of Fame was on the other line to inform the longtime Gonzaga coach he was being enshrined as part of the 2026 class, alongside NBA coaches Doc Rivers and Mike D’Antoni, former NBA star Amar’e Stoudemire, former WNBA stars Candace Parker, Elena Delle Donne and Chamique Holdsclaw, the 1996 USA women’s Olympic team and referee Joey Crawford.

“It happened in the perfect place,” Few recalled on Friday during a news conference at Mohegan Sun Casino. “… I just felt my heart dropped down to my knees and I was just kind of overwhelmed with gratitude. It was showering down on me. Your entire basketball experiences of your life comes and flashes through your mind and it was really, really powerful stuff.”

Months after learning he’d be part of the esteemed group in Springfield, Massachusetts, Few acknowledged he was still in the processing phase – and may never leave it.

“This weekend, it’s really sinking it with just the enormity of it,” Few said. “But I don’t know if it will ever truly sink in. As we’ve gotten closer and closer to this, I’ve definitely thought about that but it still seems overwhelming. Kind of surreal.”

Five months since inductions were announced, the newest Hall of Fame class will go through its enshrinement process this weekend with a full schedule of activities in Uncasville, Connecticut, and Springfield, Massachusetts.

Few and other class members went through media obligations on Friday at Mohegan Sun Casino, followed by a red carpet ceremony in the evening where he was presented with the classic Naismith Orange jackets. The Gonzaga coach responsible for 773 career victories, a winning percentage of .832 and two national championship appearances will deliver his official speech on Saturday at the “Birthplace of Basketball” in Springfield.

Between 130 and 150 people in the Gonzaga/Few circle (including plus-ones) were scheduled to attend one or both days of activities this weekend.

The group that arrived for Friday’s red carpet gala featured more than a dozen former Gonzaga players, including John Stockton, Domantas Sabonis, Drew Timme, Matt Santangelo, Dan Dickau, Zach Norvell Jr., Kevin Pangos, Jeremy Jones, Kyle Dranginis, Casey Calvary, David Stockton and Mike Nilson, to name a handful.

A large group of Few’s close coaching colleagues also made the trip out East, including Tommy Lloyd, Dan Monson, Brian Michaelson, Roger Powell, RJay Barsh, Ray Giacoletti, Bill Grier and Tad Boyle.

Others who’ve impacted Few’s life and coaching career in a significant way traveled for the weekend festivities. That contingent included former ESPN anchor Neil Everett, former Oregon athletics director Pat Kilkenny and Gonzaga benefactors Pat Volkar and Phil McCarthey.

“Just to be such a small part of this program and everything he’s built, it’s so cool and special,” said Timme, the program’s career scoring leader. “I can’t think of a more fitting way to celebrate coach Few than being here in the Hall of Fame.”

Gonzaga.title: With sudden need at point guard, Gonzaga turned to Dayton's Javon Bennett: 'Right off the bat, I wanted to play there'
Gonzaga.summary:
Trying to make sense of the last five months, Javon Bennett was recently asked how he might have reacted had someone told the Dayton transfer in March he’d be on a Zoom call with an active Hall of Fame coach recruiting the former zero-star prospect to play for a preseason top-15 Gonzaga program.

“I would think you’re insane, to be honest,” Bennett said.

Five months ago, the odds of that seemed particularly low, if not somewhere closer to zero.

First and foremost, Gonzaga didn’t have a pressing need at Bennett’s position with the expected return of starting point guard Mario Saint-Supery. Mark Few’s program was also anticipating the arrival of German prospect Jack Kayil, a hybrid guard who would’ve handled primary ball-handling duties when Saint-Supery was on the bench.

But by the time Bennett heard from Few’s coaching staff, things had changed in a fairly substantial way – both for the veteran point guard and Gonzaga’s backcourt.

Kayil’s surprising decision to stay in the NBA draft came roughly two months before Saint-Supery stunned college basketball with a mid-summer move to Spanish ACB club Valencia. The Zags had a commitment from French point guard Nathan De Sousa, but that solution felt shaky at best. The 23-year-old remains in limbo waiting on the NCAA to approve his eligibility waiver.

Things were starting to shift in Bennett’s life, too.

The guard who played 136 games over four seasons at Merrimack and Dayton had completed one NBA workout with his hometown team, the Orlando Magic, when agent Harrison Gaines recommended he put the pre-draft process on pause.

There was a small chance Bennett and other graduates of the high school class of 2022 would get another shot at college basketball through new NCAA legislation allowing athletes to play five seasons over five years.

It was worth exploring, so Bennett, who was also garnering interest from multiple professional clubs in Germany and one in Romania, joined a lawsuit in Ohio with other college basketball players seeking a fifth year. In early July, he and his father flew from Orlando to Cincinnati to sit in on a hearing where Bennett and five other players watched and listened to Ryan Downton present the plaintiffs’ case to Judge Christopher Wagner.

“It was definitely tense,” Bennett said. “That was my first time being inside of a courtroom, especially during the jury. … It was a long day.”

The hearing lasted roughly five hours and Bennett had to wait another full week for the ruling. He was scrolling social media when he saw the news that Wagner had granted a preliminary injunction, guaranteeing another year of eligibility to the players involved in the suit. Downton followed up with an email to confirm the ruling, and Bennett promptly called his father at work to share the news.

“Once it got passed, it kind of just felt like recruitment again,” Bennett said. “I had to wait for college coaches to call me and see what fit and where I was going to play. Gonzaga was definitely an interest when they called and kind of just right off the bat, I knew I wanted to play there.”

It’s another unlikely step in Bennett’s basketball journey. Although he set a school record with 2,147 career points at Trinity Prep in the Orlando, Florida, area, Bennett was unrated on national scouting services and had one “legit” Division I offer from Merrimack. Another school in his home state, Florida Gulf Coast, technically offered the guard after he attended their summer camp, but the coaching staff eventually lost contact with Bennett, leaving just the one D-I option.

He started in 27 of 34 games as a freshman at Merrimack, guiding the Warriors to a Northeast Conference Tournament championship while averaging 9.6 points and 3.4 assists. In their fourth year transitioning from Division II to Division I, the Warriors weren’t able to take the league’s NCAA Tournament bid, forfeiting the spot to NEC runner-up Fairleigh Dickinson.

Bennett moved on to Dayton, instantly becoming a fan favorite for Anthony Grant’s program, starting all but four games over three seasons while leading the Flyers to an NCAA Tournament appearance in 2024 and consecutive NIT berths in 2025 and 2026. The point guard averaged 15.8 ppg and 2.9 apg last season at Dayton while turning in 11 games of 20 points or more.

A 1,565-point career scorer who posted a win-loss record of 91-47 at Merrimack and Dayton, Bennett always felt he could contribute to a high-major program capable of playing for a national championship, but the dream didn’t materialize until a handful of weeks ago when he heard from Gonzaga General Manager Kurt Bambauer.

“I know for me, I’ve always envisioned this. It’s funny how it happened,” said Bennett, who earned All-Atlantic 10 first-team honors last season. “You would think it would happen by my senior year and I wouldn’t have to come back to college after this. Just with the circumstances, I know this was a long time coming for me and I know the work I’ve put in.

“Everybody that’s close to me knows they’ve helped me through the journey and know this is where I wanted to be at and this is where I could play at. It’s been a great journey from where I started to now and having a chance to obviously compete for a national championship is huge.”

Bambauer organized Zoom calls with other members of Gonzaga’s coaching staff, who pulled up film of Ryan Nembhard to give Bennett a better idea of how the program’s point guards operate.

“If you told me I was going to go to Gonzaga after I left Dayton, I would be like, ‘No, there’s no way,’ ” Bennett said. “The relationship we’ve been able to build with the staff in these last couple weeks has been great. We’ve done Zooms and I’ve been talking to them basically every day. We’re just excited on both ends to get this started.”

Pending his eligibility waiver, De Sousa could still be in the fold at Gonzaga next season and coaches told Bennett they were still browsing the “5-in-5” transfer market, potentially looking to add another lead guard to the 2026-27 roster.

“I know for me, wherever I go I want to go where I can play and I can make an impact,” Bennett said. “At the end of the day, if they do bring somebody, if they don’t bring somebody, I just want to show what I can do.”

Bennett is currently back home in Orlando going through a two-a-day training cycle. Mornings typically begin with a shooting workout, followed immediately by a lift. He returns to the gym around 5 p.m. for a second workout with trainer T.J. Bannister, a former college player at Virginia and Liberty.

“I’ve been basically doing that the whole summer,” Bennett said.

The veteran guard will be moving his life from one corner of the country to the other when he flies to Spokane next Thursday. Bennett, a low-turnover point guard who ranked top five in Atlantic 10 scoring last season, looks forward to facilitating for Gonzaga’s frontcourt, which is expected to be one of the most talented in the country with the return of Braden Huff and addition of transfer center Massamba Diop.

“Diop had a great year at ASU and he’s due for a big year this year and he’s been working,” Bennett said. “I know Huff has been returning and he’s ready to be a player of the year contender. I just want to make his job a lot easier when we play, so that’s kind of my whole thought process, just help the team win and make it easy for those guys.”

Bennett feels his passing is still an underrated aspect of his game and said he’s been working heavily on pick-and-roll reads with his trainer back home in Florida. In terms of college games played, Bennett will be the most experienced player on GU’s roster – pending other additions – and feels his leadership will be a valuable tool.

“Obviously staying sharp on my shooting and making sure I stay consistent with that and like I said, my leadership as well,” Bennett said. “Definitely improve on that with the amount of younger guys we have on this team, I can definitely bring a level of experience and leadership to that.”
