Washington State.title: 'Whatever you sow, you will reap': The patience behind Branden Ganashamoorthy's arrival in WSU's receiver corps
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN – At first, Emma Ganashamoorthy felt a rush of relief, thinking her son was only joking. She was on the phone with Branden, her oldest child, a burgeoning wide receiver at Washington State. It was the spring of last year, and the Cougars were close to wrapping up their spring practice slate.

But it was April Fool’s Day, so Emma figured Branden had a trick up his sleeve.

“Hey mom, I broke my ankle,” he told her.

“What?” she replied.

“April fools,” he said. “Not.”

Turns out, Branden really had broken his ankle, which had finally succumbed to a previous injury he had suffered in the season before. He missed the rest of the Cougars’ spring practices, later underwent surgery and missed part of the ensuing fall camp.

“You’ve come from, you’ve just killed it in the middle of spring ball,” Emma said, “to, you can’t even walk for weeks. That’s definitely a change.”

It was more than just a change. It was a crushing development for Ganashamoorthy, whose WSU career had seemed to follow the same script for each of his first two-plus seasons with the program: One step forward, two back. He was a freak athlete, so his name came up constantly in practice settings. Did you see that catch from BG? How about that move?

Ever since arriving on campus as a walk-on in 2023, competing in track for one season before dropping it to focus on football, Ganashamoorthy knew what he was capable of, knew that his sheer speed and size would help him crack the receiver rotation at some point. In his quieter moments, though, he heard the doubts whisper in his ear.

“Injuries can destroy that confidence, you know?” Ganashamoorthy said. “Honestly, like when I was coming back and then it started hurting again, I kinda was just like, ‘Do I still got it?’ ”

In the time that followed, Ganashamoorthy saw reasons to believe the doubts. He returned in time for the 2025 season, but he saw limited playing time that fall. To this day, you can count on two hands the number of passes he has caught at the college level: 10 receptions for 87 yards and one touchdown, which came in the 2024 Holiday Bowl. Even when he got his opportunities, they didn’t work out in his favor: a ball overthrown, thrown at his feet, a penalty by a teammate, you name it. He may have excelled as a run-blocker, finishing last season tops on the team in Pro Football Focus’ run-blocking grades among wide receivers, but it wasn’t the vision he saw for himself.

Did he really belong?

“It’s hard in the moment,” Ganashamoorthy said, “but, I mean, it pays off at some point.”

That point may have arrived. Ahead of his redshirt junior season, Ganashamoorthy has enjoyed by far his best fall camp as a Cougar, perhaps the best individual camp of anyone on the team. On one of the first days of practice, he used one hand to haul in a catch . Running with WSU’s first- and second-team units, he’s hauled in more catches than you can count: some sliding, others diving, still others leaping and leaning and contorting like a circus performer.

Ganashamoorthy – simply “BG” to his teammates and coaches – has looked sharper than ever, faster than ever, stronger than ever. A Monroe native, he used this summer to find the right weightlifting regimen, a delicate balance between gaining muscle and maintaining speed. He’s walked a fine line, making sure that his new lifting program doesn’t strip him of the speed that made him a track star in his high school days at Eastside Catholic. It’s led him here, to the doorstep of his fourth season in crimson and gray laundry.

He spent his first three mired in change that swept across the program, across a young Ganashamoorthy, like a hurricane. In 2023, halfway through his third day of fall camp , former conference members Washington and Oregon decided to leave, collapsing the league in traditional form. About a year later, the coach who recruited him, Jake Dickert, also left. And a year after that, new coach Jimmy Rogers did the same, hitting Ganashamoorthy and the Cougars’ program with another bout of instability.

Is this the year Ganashamoorthy finally breaks into the Cougs’ wideout rotation? Will he get meaningful snaps when WSU kicks off its season next Sunday at No. 17 Washington? He certainly has the momentum. During fall camp, he was a fixture in the top two units on offense, indicating he isn’t far off. He’s in a room with plenty of talent, from Oregon State transfer Darrius Clemons to Missouri transfer Daniel Blood to veteran returner Tony Freeman. Is there room for him?

If anyone has earned the right to feel that there should be, it’s Ganashamoorthy, who earned a scholarship this spring. To get to such a point, though, he had to weave another adventure entirely.

• • •

Mornings at Harmony Farms start early. The owner of the operation, Emma would wake up the earliest, at around 4:45 or 5 a.m., and her three kids would follow: Branden, Hannah and Caden. They would saunter into the kitchen and find a list split into three categories: outside chores, inside chores and schoolwork.

Inside chores were the simplest, easier tasks like laundry, sweeping, vacuuming, dishes, dusting. Branden and his two siblings were homeschooled until their freshman years of high school. When he was growing up, he always remembered his friends’ reactions when he would tell them he was homeschooled – “Oh, you’re weird,” he would hear often – but he took pride in where he came from, in having a mother he could look up to so strongly.

But the most unique part of all, the part that set the tone for the next chapter of Ganashamoorthy’s life, centered around the outside chores. They mostly revolved around taking care of the horses on the farm. Some stay at the farm for boarding. Others are there for training. One belongs to Emma. All of them need to be cared for, though, which is where Branden and his siblings often came in.

When it was his turn to feed the horses, he would get up a little before 6 a.m. and head out. Sometimes they would get grain, other times they would get hay. He would often share the duties with his sister, Hannah, who found herself fonder of the horses than her younger brother. Even when Branden would get home in the evening because of track practice, he still tended to the horses, blanketing them and cleaning water troughs. He rarely complained. “Maybe when it was pouring with rain and he had to go put horse blankets on,” Emma said, “but that was about it.”

“That’s all I knew was to work hard and be consistent,” Branden said. “I saw it every day from my mom, and so I take that now. People don’t see the first three years that I was here, but people see what I’m doing now. But I’ve been doing the same thing, being consistent every single day. It just happens to be under the spotlight now, you know?”

“That’s the biggest thing is literally just watching her work hard every single day, every day, Monday through Sunday. That’s kinda just instilled in me,” he added. “If you see something or see someone you look up to, and like they’re doing something to the max they can do it, you want to be like them, you know? It drives you.”

In between chores, Branden and his siblings kept growing up in the ways that would shape the rest of their young adult lives. Out in the other five acres of the family’s 10-acre property, the part tucked into a forest and away from the horses, Branden and his friends would build huts. Tree houses. His younger brother, Caden, would often join. They would spend hours in there, no phones, no internet, just friends and siblings bonding like the year was 1999.

“Basically,” Branden said, “we would just be in the woods every day.”

In the house, the siblings would turn just about everything into a competition. A young Branden was beginning to get interested in track, so he and Hannah would pull couch cushions off the sofa and use them to set up courses in the house so they could race. They would see who could get dressed the fastest. When Branden and Caden would play cards, things got so heated that the loser usually ended up throwing the cards at the winner in frustration.

Two years younger, Branden usually lost to his sister at games they would set up. It happened so often, Hannah said, that eventually Branden stopped wanting to compete against her. “I don’t win anything!” he would say. “I’m not gonna do it.”

When she thinks back now though, Hannah sees a deeper truth about her brother.

“I think at that point it bred in him this … I don’t know,” she said, searching for the right description. “This hunger to want to win at everything.”

“It’s his discipline,” Caden said. “Just the way he lives, his discipline is so sharp. It’s insane. There’s certain levels. I’ll be eating this, I’ll be eating that, and he’ll be like, ‘Dude, don’t eat that.’ His discipline has definitely got him to where he’s at, especially with how frequently he works out before 6 a.m. We usually do devotions at night, at like 10 o’clock, and my mom will be like, ‘We can’t call Branden because he’s still at the facility training by himself catching footballs.’ I would be like, ‘That’s crazy.’ ”

• • •

Since his arrival on campus in the fall of 2023, the list of people who have showered Ganashamoorthy with praise read like a who’s-who of notable Washington State football figures of recent.

Take a look for yourself.

There’s former wide receiver Kyle Williams, who was drafted by the New England Patriots in the third round in 2025. “BG, he’s just an overall athlete,” Williams said after one fall camp practice in 2023. “He can go up and grab the ball. He’s long. I mean, he still has to learn, but his route-running is there.”

There’s former head coach Jake Dickert, who saw Ganashamoorthy’s potential around the same time, back in 2023. “He has no idea what he’s doing, and it is awesome,” Dickert said. “I mean, it is awesome to watch him come out here and just every day get better. We just went over personnel yesterday on the off day – we’re excited about BG and his development and what he can do. I’m not gonna put a ceiling on him.”

There’s former quarterback Zevi Eckhaus, the Cougars’ backup in 2024 and starter in 2025. “I think one that definitely stands out the top of my head that I can think of is BG, Branden Ganashamoorthy,” Eckhaus said in December 2024, thinking about younger players he was impressed by. “He was a guy that was rolling with me on the twos throughout the year. He’s definitely had more of an elevated role with the absence of Kris Hutson and Trey Leckner. I’m excited to see him go out there and make some plays. He touched the field a little bit throughout the year, but obviously with the absence of those guys that we’ve lost, I think he’ll have a higher role, and I’m excited to see him go out there and play.”

There’s former offensive coordinator Ben Arbuckle, who worked with Ganashamoorthy in his first two seasons. “BG, he’s been making plays and being really consistent,” Arbuckle said after one fall camp practice in 2024. “He’s elevating himself into that conversation of a guy that we can depend on.”

There’s former wide receivers coach Nick Edwards, who coached Ganashamoorthy the same two seasons: “He works hard every day,” Edwards said in August 2024, drawing out each word for emphasis. “He cares about this sport. He was a track guy, and now he’s converted into a football player, and he just wants to make sure that he can go ahead and prove to himself and to us that he’s that guy. He’s been doing a great job of catching the ball and getting off press, and being long and athletic and being a really good vertical threat down the field.”

Then finally, Dickert had this to say about Ganashamoorthy in August 2024. “BG, in that team breakdown, he took the step from being a track athlete to finally being a football player,” Dickert said. “And I’m proud of that kid. It was really good to see.”

All of which has cast two truths over Ganashamoorthy and his long journey: He’s been capable of a breakout season for years. And it has taken a mountain of patience to stay ready for it.

In truth, Ganashamoorthy says, he would be lying if he said the thought of leaving Washington State never crossed his mind. How could he not? The first head coach he played for now coaches two time zones away. The second departed after less than a calendar year in Pullman. He’s had three different head coaches, three different position group coaches, hundreds of different teammates, many of whom are now scattered across the map with different programs, different walks of life.

“There’s probably many nights where, he never was ever going to quit, but he really was probably frustrated at times,” Emma said, “because he knew what he would be capable of being able to do.”

It raises what feels like a fair question: What made Ganashamoorthy want to stay at WSU through all that?

The answer is the key to understanding what has given Ganashamoorthy the patience to wait his turn. For one, he says, he has always heard from his new wide receivers coach soon after they’ve taken over. That’s made him feel reassured, that his spot is safe and his presence is appreciated on the new team.

Secondly, though, he has always taken deep pride in one thing above all: his work ethic. He remembers the early mornings on the farm, the 50-minute drives from Monroe to Eastside Catholic for his senior year of high school, the work it took just to earn a roster spot that season, which propelled him forward to WSU. “Putting in work was never an issue with Branden,” said Dwayne Pocknett, a longtime family friend and an Eastside Catholic coach.

For Ganashamoorthy, the days he spent on the scout team live vividly in his head. “Those days are hard, man,” he said, “especially when it’s cold.” He remembers feeling so far behind, both mentally and physically, one field over from where the Cougars’ starters practice. He saw some teammates going through the motions.

But he also remembers connecting with former cornerbacks coach Ray Brown, who now coaches the same position for the San Francisco 49ers. Back then, Brown told Ganashamoorthy this: “You take these reps intentionally, you do everything intentionally when you’re on scout team, you will see the results.”

“So that really flipped the switch,” Ganashamoorthy said. “Like oh, I could just go through the motions out here. Or no, I could go 100% every play and not only get myself better, but get the other people better. I definitely saw the fruit from that. You may sow those seeds then, which was three years ago, and you may see the results now, which is three and a half years later. It talks about that in the Bible. Whatever you sow, you will reap. But you just have to be patient in the time being, so that’s what kept me going, honestly.”

Three years later, Ganashamoorthy may finally have earned what he longed for for so long, a spot on the field as a wide receiver, a consistent role in the pass-catching department. It eluded him for three trips around the sun. A fourth seems to be arriving at the right time. No April fools.

Washington State.title: Bill Doba, who led legendary Washington State defenses before becoming head coach, dies at 85
Washington State.summary:
Bill Doba, the celebrated former Washington State defensive coordinator who later served as the Cougars head coach for five years in the 2000s, died Friday, the school announced. He was 85.

Doba had suffered a stroke last weekend, according to a report from Cougfan.com. He was living in southwestern Michigan, where he had resided for the past two decades after spending 19 years at WSU.

Doba compiled a 30-29 record as WSU’s head coach from 2003-07, leading the Cougars to 10 wins and a memorable Holiday Bowl victory over fifth-ranked Texas in his first season. He earned Pac-10 Coach of the Year honors in 2003, and WSU was ranked No. 9 in the nation in the final AP poll.

The Cougars didn’t reach those heights again during his final four years as head coach, but Doba has remained a beloved figure among Washington State supporters for his endearing personality, long stretch of success on the Palouse and commitment to the school. He stayed connected with WSU after stepping down from the head-coaching job following the 2007 season, often returning to Pullman for games and booster events and acting as a representative for the Cougars. He attended a 2022 celebration of the 1997 Rose Bowl team, raised the Ol’ Crimson WSU flag before last year’s Apple Cup and waved the flag during an ESPN GameDay program in 2024.

“The opportunity (WSU) gave me to make a few bucks and be able to help my kids and grandkids with things in their lives is something I’ll always be grateful for,” Doba told The Spokesman-Review in 2012. “And where else can you live where you can walk to work to play Southern Cal on Saturday?

“When the Realtor asked for the keys to the house, I had no idea where they were. I’d never locked it or my truck. I had a great time. I just wish we could have finished stronger.”

Doba joined coach Mike Price’s WSU staff in 1989 as a linebackers coach and oversaw that unit until he was promoted to Cougars defensive coordinator in 1994. That year, he orchestrated the famed “Palouse Posse” defense, one of the best defensive units in college football history, which led the nation in total defense. Price called Doba “one of the best defensive coaches in the country” during a 2022 interview with The S-R.

“We had a deal in preseason scrimmages: Wherever the ball ended up, if it was a long pass, if it was caught or not, all 11 had to sprint as hard as they could to the ball,” Doba told The S-R in 2022 of his defensive coaching. “If I caught a guy loafing, they went off the field and the 2s came in.”

In 1997, Doba’s fourth year as Cougs DC, the team made its first Rose Bowl appearance in 67 years and finished with 10 wins. Doba also instructed WSU’s defense in a Sun Bowl-winning campaign in 2001 and during the 2002 season, which saw WSU win 10 games and make another Rose Bowl appearance. He then became WSU’s head coach in 2003 after Price left the school to take the head-coaching job at Alabama.

“You’re a really great friend of mine and I can always depend on you,” Price told Doba during the 2022 celebration of the 1997 Rose Bowl team.

“Bill was a great coach, person and father and he cared about the kids (on the team) like they were his own,” Price told Cougfan. “He was so good to me and so perfect at that time in my career as a head coach. He was a leading light for us. He was somethin’ else.”

After his 10-win campaign in his first year as WSU coach, Doba’s team went 5-6 in 2004, with three losses coming by one possession. WSU then compiled a 4-7 record in 2005, went 6-6 in 2006 and 5-7 in 2007. Doba guided the Cougars to three Apple Cup victories as head coach.

Doba was born in South Bend, Indiana. He played halfback and defensive back at Ball State in nearby Muncie. Doba began his coaching career in 1962 as an assistant at Goshen High in Indiana. He served as the school’s head coach from 1968-70 before a six-year stay as coach at Mishawaka High (Indiana) before beginning his collegiate coaching career in 1977 as an assistant under Lee Corso at Indiana. He coached for the Hoosiers for six years, then worked as an assistant for another four years at Purdue before a two-year stop at the Citadel in Charleston, South Carolina, where he coordinated the defense. Doba then began his long tenure at WSU.

Bill and Judy Doba were married for 43 years after meeting in college. Judy died in 2006 following a battle with cancer. The couple had three children.

Countless former Cougars who played for Doba shared heartfelt reactions over social media to the coach’s passing.

“Love you and will miss you Coach!!” former WSU quarterback Ryan Leaf posted on X.

“One of the greatest men I’ve ever been around,” former QB Alex Brink wrote on X. “Such an incredible impact on so many people. Thank you Coach.”

“Today we lost a true Cougar legend,” Lewis and Clark High grad and former WSU safety Erik Coleman posted on Instagram. “More importantly, I lost a coach who played a tremendous role in shaping me, not just as a football player, but as a man. You always told us the truth, whether we wanted to hear it or not. You demanded accountability, toughness, and character. Those lessons have stayed with me long after my playing days ended. … Your impact reaches far beyond wins and losses. You helped shape the lives of so many young men.”

How WSU safety Jeremiah Bernard battled his own pressure and ascended into the Cougars' starting lineup
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN – Jeremiah Bernard laughs and drops his head when the topic of his new home comes up, his medium-length locs swinging down and obscuring his smile. In the first two years of his career at Cal Poly, which is situated in a central-California town called San Luis Obispo, he enjoyed all kinds of hobbies.

He liked going to the beach, taking a short 15-minute drive along Highway 101 to Avila Beach. He’s into fashion, so he’d often venture to the malls San Luis Obispo offers to look for new clothes. And he loves playing basketball, enjoys jumping into pick-up games around campus.

Washington State, where he transferred over the winter to play safety, isn’t exactly brimming with those types of amenities. Pullman doesn’t have a mall, doesn’t have a movie theater, certainly doesn’t have a beach, unless you count a collection of sand dunes around the Snake River about 30 miles west of town. The town is more or less famous for, well, being more distraction-free.

“Pullman is still beautiful for sure,” Bernard said. “It’s just a different type of vibe.”

Get to know Bernard, though, and you learn that a different type of vibe is what he’s all about. When he hit the portal last December, looking to ascend to the FBS level, he held deep convictions on what he was looking for. He wanted a place to develop, a place where he could stay away from distractions, a place where he could trust his coaches.

That’s the main reason he wound up at WSU, where he’s expected to start at safety for a Cougar defense that cemented itself as the story of the team’s fall camp earlier this month. He really trusts cornerbacks coach Brandyn Thompson, who worked the same job last season at Cal Poly, where the two first connected. The two got in touch and Thompson invited him on an official visit, where Bernard “fell in love instantly,” he said.

There’s plenty Bernard liked about WSU. His father, Marcus, liked the combination of a big-time feel with a family atmosphere. Most of Jeremiah’s reasons centered around the Cougar coaching staff, he said, and how the Washington State orbit differed from those of higher-profile places – “with the portal, the bigger the school, the more politics,” he said back in the spring.

But at the heart of Bernard’s rise, central to his ability to parlay a two-year stay at a middling FCS program into a starting spot at a Pac-12 school, is what’s important to him. For this, he credits his parents, Marcus and Topaiz, who began steering him in the right direction from a young age.

“They instilled in me not to get caught up in all the lights and all the money,” Bernard said. “You know how this NIL thing goes. A lot of kids can fall for that trap, but I feel like that was my main thing. Like, I don’t wanna fall for it. I wanna go somewhere where I can be successful and actually get that opportunity to be the player I know I can be. And that was my main thing, making that transition from the lower level of FCS to now FBS.”

But to understand how Bernard put himself in a position to make that transition, we have to understand how he managed his inner monologue, how he forgave himself for not doing it earlier in life.

Bernard was a freshman when he made the play of his life, the best sequence he’s authored in all his time. This was in 2024, and in a tight game between Cal Poly and Sacramento State, Bernard’s Mustangs were barely hanging on to a three-point lead. With about 90 seconds to go, the Hornets were driving, threatening to take the lead inside the red zone.

On one play, Sac State quarterback Carson Conklin scrambled from the pocket and surged toward the end zone. He had nothing but green grass ahead of him. He powered to the 5-yard line, only a couple strides from taking the lead, so close to handing Cal Poly another frustrating loss.

That’s about when Bernard soared into the picture, diving toward Conklin and stripping the ball clean. A teammate fell on the fumble. Cal Poly won in dramatic fashion.

“That just catapulted him into his second year,” Bernard’s father, Marcus, said.

But what really tied Bernard’s first and second years at Cal Poly together was something else: losing. In Bernard’s two seasons with the Mustangs, where he was coached by former WSU skipper Paul Wulff, the team went a combined 7-16. As a freshman, Bernard and the Mustangs once dropped five in a row. As a sophomore, they suffered a six-game slide. Two of those victories came over Western Oregon, a Division II outfit.

Bernard made all kinds of plays, but it didn’t matter for Cal Poly, which wasn’t good enough to capitalize. Last fall, Bernard secured four interceptions and six pass breakups, remarkable numbers for a safety. Still, the Mustangs triumphed over just three Division-I teams, winning just two Big Sky Conference games that season.

Take a look when Bernard made his biggest splashes. He broke up two passes against Montana, which earned a 28-9 win. He intercepted a pass against Portland State, but that ended in a 40-35 loss. He picked off another pass against Northern Arizona, which went on to take a 35-27 win, and added one more against Montana State, a 34-17 defeat for the Mustangs.

There were some exceptions – he picked off a pass in a win over Sacramento State, and he did the same in a victory over Eastern Washington – but for Cal Poly, the losses far outnumbered the wins. It took a toll on Bernard, who internalized the lessons on a deeper level: Even if I ball out, there’s still a decent chance we’ll lose.

“As a DB group, we had to be perfect almost every game,” Bernard said.

Bernard began to understand that at an even earlier age. At Modesto Christian, where he played on the varsity squad from 2021-23, the Crusaders languished. In Bernard’s sophomore year, they went 1-7. In his junior season, they improved to 6-5. Then in Bernard’s senior campaign, Modesto Christian regressed to just 2-8, for a total record of 9-20. Bernard and the Crusaders ended his senior year with seven straight losses.

Somewhere along the way, Bernard felt two truths pull at him. One: He had to be perfect. Two: Even if he was, his team might still lose the game. The second might feel like a mature lesson to learn, but thanks to the first, he began to internalize a sense of burden when he stepped out onto the field on gamedays.

It’s not a particularly healthy mentality for anyone at age 17, let alone Bernard, who is already hard on himself. After lots of his games at Cal Poly, he would call Marcus and reflect on the game. It wouldn’t be too long before Jeremiah started to critique himself.

“He does put a lot of pressure on himself,” Marcus said. “He can have a great game, and he’ll still say, you know, Dad, I should have done this, this, this, A, B and C.”

“He put so much pressure on himself to try to do whatever he could to help the team win,” added Topaiz, Jeremiah’s mother. “He really put himself out there a few games, especially against Sac State, our local rival here in Nor Cal. He’s pumping everyone else up. ‘We are not losing this game.’ So he put a lot of weight on himself because they were losing. He would try everything.”

Here, Marcus and Topaiz’s influence shines through like sunlight through stain-glass windows. When Jeremiah was a kid, he would study hard for a test, head into the classroom and walk out with a score of 87. “Mom,” he would say, “I only got an 87. I don’t know what happened.”

Then Topaiz would smile and reassure her son. “An 87?” she would say. “Isn’t that good?”

When she zooms out, Topaiz realizes that those are the kinds of moments that helped her son get over the hump, to let the frustration sit for a moment before bouncing back.

“You need to recover faster,” Topaiz would tell Jeremiah and his three siblings. “So have your moment. Don’t ignore the way you feel. But that was one of our themes for a long time – recover faster. Let’s not stay here. He’s good at that, and he also knows how to encourage other people out of it and to try to be positive.”

Still, Bernard kept his head up by always reminding himself of a couple things. One involved his high school recruitment. Out of Modesto Christian, he fielded just two offers, both from FCS schools: UC Davis and Cal Poly. In the dog days of his time with the Mustangs, when the losses piled up in bunches, he kept that in mind. That fueled him, he says, but it also gave him a sense of gratitude.

The second thing Bernard reminded himself of took some time to develop, a sense that he belonged at the college level, that he could play. He felt a twinge of that when he came up with his game-winning forced fumble back in 2024, but it didn’t really set in until the next season. In the final four games of his Cal Poly career, he snagged three interceptions, a torrid pace.

“That last little run,” Bernard said, “once I got like the one in the middle, I was like, ‘OK, this is gonna keep going from here.’ That was like my moment. I’m like, ‘All right, I can do this.’ ”

At WSU, Bernard has only shown more signs that, all right, he can do this.

When Bernard arrived at Washington State, defensive coordinator Trent Bray thought he had an idea of his new safety’s game. He loved Bernard’s ability as a run-stopper. He knew he was a hard-hitter.

“He has improved his coverage probably drastically since he got here,” Bray said, “so he’s really impressed me with his improvement that way.”

Bray had a front-row seat to that development on Aug. 10, the fourth day of the Cougars’ fall camp. Bernard and WSU’s first-team defense were on the field against its first-team offense. On one play, a pass sailed in Bernard’s direction, so the 20-year-old safety whisked that way and reached out his arms.

Then came his legs. Bernard leaped and went fully horizontal in the air, laying out to break up a pass, looking more like a superhero than a mere mortal in that moment. He bounced back up to his feet in a second. It was a sweltering day in Pullman, temperatures rising into the upper-80s, but Bernard played like he had a personal AC unit tucked inside his helmet.

During fall camp, Bernard made too many plays like that to count. In both of the Cougars’ scrimmages, the only times they’ve had the green light to tackle in earnest, he’s delivered a number of brutal hits. When the ball is snapped, he’ll hover in the secondary, spot where the play is headed, then slam the gas like he’s behind a Ferrari, flooding into the backfield for a blistering hit.

“In the actual practice where we’re thud or tag, we have to kinda pull him back,” Bray said after the team’s first scrimmage. “So today was good to let him just unleash and go out and hit, and he did.”

“I’ve always kinda just been a playmaker,” Bernard said. “I’ve always tried to be around the ball and make plays. That’s always been my thing. So I don’t really think of it as like, oh yeah, like guys, we should shy away from it. I feel like if you have guys in the room, they’re gonna have that same mindset. They want the play to come to them. They want to be the one to make that play.”

This fall, Bernard will certainly be one of those guys. He just might not have the chance to decompress at the beach.

Washington State.title: 1.21 jigowatts of positive energy: How first-year coach Kirby Moore's upbeat personality can take WSU to brighter future
Washington State.summary:
Kirby Moore does a funny thing when he gets ready to address the media. He’ll walk up to the collection of reporters, whether standing up after practice or sitting down for a more formal news conference, and he does something different.

Instead of waiting for everyone to get set, to receive his first question, he starts chatting. He’ll offer a brief overview of what’s been going on around the program – summer workouts, fall camp, a player’s hot stretch, whatever – and then proceed with things. “Any questions?” he’ll say.

It’s a humorous way for Moore to get things started. He might not mean for it to be, but it does highlight a part of his personality, an element to what makes Moore, well, Moore: His bright character, the way his positive energy imbues a Cougar program that needs a little bit of that in its current era.

Notably, it stands in stark contrast to his predecessor. Former head coach Jimmy Rogers, who decamped after one season for the same job at Iowa State, did some nice things with the Cougars. He made a bowl game, extending the program’s streak, and he gave Power 4 foes Virginia and Ole Miss legitimate scares on the road. But one thing he didn’t seem to place much importance on centered on his outward expressions, carrying a middling energy around in media availabilities, public speaking opportunities and the like.

Before we can assess his head coaching ability, that seems to be the biggest difference between the two head coaches. Moore’s energy stands out like a skyscraper in a Palouse wheat field, perhaps offering a glimpse into the kind of offense he’s bringing to the Cougs’ program.

“He brought some things he’d seen at Missouri, and then kinda put his little twist on it, his little swag on it, I guess,” said senior wide receiver Daniel Blood, a transfer from Missouri, where Moore worked the previous three seasons as offensive coordinator. “So some things are the same, and then some things are just, his swag put on it.”

A native of nearby Prosser, Moore certainly earned the opportunity. His first job was in 2014 as the College of Idaho’s wide receivers coach, which he parlayed into a GA gig at Washington for the 2015-16 seasons. Then he moved on to Fresno State, where he coached wideouts for four seasons before taking over the offensive coordinator reins in 2022, which helped propel him to the same job with the Tigers, with whom he worked from 2023-25.

Since he’s arrived at WSU, which has been picked to finish around the middle of the rebuilt Pac-12, he’s infused the same kind of energy in all his interactions.

“The biggest thing is that he treats us like adults, and he treats us like we’re pros,” wide receiver Branden Ganashamoorthy said. “If you’re not gonna go to certain things, there’s consequences for those certain things, just like in the next level. He has a great philosophy of ‘this play.’ And a lot of people don’t understand – football is such a mental sport. You gotta play this play. If you think about the next play or the play behind you, you’re gonna mess up. I think he instills a great culture and a great just ‘this play’ philosophy that is so important to players and to the staff. He takes care of us, and he takes care of the staff like the best I’ve ever had.”

Perhaps the best evidence comes from the players, the foundation of the program and the engine that makes the whole thing go. He’s joked before that as much as he loves his staff, they won’t be the ones making plays on Saturdays. The players are.

That mentality certainly stood out to quarterback Caden Pinnick, who will likely earn the starting role when WSU’s season-opener at rival Washington rolls around. He was coveted by Colorado, but after taking a visit to WSU in the winter, he decided to commit.

“When I first got here, coach Moore stood out to me the most,” Pinnick said after one spring practice. “It was kinda that leadership kind of feeling. He didn’t overly show that he was a head coach. You know, he was very humble, very relaxed. Came and introduced him to me and my mom, very nice to my mom. So that spoke levels.”

Still, the best example of Moore’s light personality came at the beginning of fall camp. A day before the Cougars embarked on the 15-practice slate, he sat in front of a group of reporters and talked about the team’s summer, about one day when the team ran up College Hill, a particularly steep slope.

In the crowd of players scaling the hill, Moore was in there, too.

“Got a couple reps in there. I was worried there at the end,” Moore joked. “I wanted to make sure that Achilles stayed intact.”

Washington State.title: WSU's future is whatever you make it, so make it a good one | CFB preview 2026
Washington State.summary:
This is a new competitive landscape, and if you’re viewing the structural changes as anything other than opportunities, you’re already losing ground.

If Washington State football fans can be patient, and keep the big-picture goals in sight, the new terrain might provide a better path to future success.

Especially for those who can remain somewhat fluid in their definition of success.

WSU’s affiliation this season continues to be called the Pacific-12 Conference, although there’s only two hold-overs from its fully loaded incarnation, with the fillers being pulled up from what had been considered leagues of lesser repute.

We may also note that the Pac-12 appellation misses the mark to the degree that it is not exclusively Pacific, and far from numerically accurate, with eight football-playing members.

Further, literally, one of the new rivals (Texas State) is located in San Marcos, Texas, roughly 2,000 miles south of Pullman, and geographically much closer to Nicaragua (1,464 miles) than it is to Spokane (2,018).

But, until the college-football shapers get real and call the major conferences ESPN, CBS, Fox and NBC – with sub-divisions called Basic Cable, Premium Cable and Streaming – we won’t quibble about still going by the Pac-12 title.

So, while the whole adaptation to the new environment may be uncomfortable and require some recalibration of identity and expectations, there may be some hidden factors that could compensate.

It may take some time, but it’s best to get over the initial feeling of relegation to a lower division.

Fans can cherish memories of historic blood-feud rivalries and great victories in the past, but those days irretrievably expired. Money has made it so.

How to spin this whole reconstitution to avoid that sense of loss?

When the conference produced its new logo in spring, it offered a few strained explanations of the look, the press release claiming it had “Superhero Energy,” and it was “Aggressive. Modern. Unapologetic.”

Less embarrassing and more to the point, it made the fair description: “Where Tradition Meets Transformation.”

Transformation. Yes. College sports have been about little else. Money, of course, having the greatest transformative powers.

Still, those with emotional ties to WSU, and most of the other schools in this new Pac-12 football fraternity, have to be heartened by recent events.

For instance, when longtime Big Ten doormat Indiana won the national championship, thrashing Alabama 38-3 in the second round of the playoffs, every traditional underdog was given reason to bark.

Vanderbilt, Tulane and James Madison finished higher than USC and Michigan and Penn State in the final polls.

In times of massive change, the old, tradition-bound institutions may become vulnerable, while creative and innovative programs can rise by being more adaptable.

WSU, with a new coaching staff and a committed administration, could be one of those programs carving a different path to the College Football Playoffs.

Keep in mind, at least one Group of Six team is reserved a place in the 12-team CFP.

Last season, two G6 teams, Tulane and James Madison, were included among the Power 4 candidates.

It’s not hard at all to see WSU in the future playing at a level with or above Tulane and James Madison.

Last season, WSU lost to James Madison, 24-20, on the road, and looked on the threshold of an upset road win.

Tulane, meanwhile, got clobbered (45-10) by Ole Miss in the regular season, while WSU pushed Ole Miss in a narrow, 24-21, road loss at Oxford, Mississippi.

Most predictions suggest the rebuilding Cougars will likely finish in the middle of the pack in the new Pac-12 this fall. Boise State and San Diego State are considered likely title contenders.

With respect, those two schools are a long way from posing the challenges that Oregon, Washington, USC, etc., the Cougars used to face.

If the goal is to win enough games to boost the win-loss record and claim a conference championship and get into the playoffs, the new Pac-12 provides far more chances than the old Pac-12.

We may then observe a best-case corollary in which WSU football treats the new Pac-12 the way Gonzaga exploited the West Coast Conference competition during the Zags’ transformation into a powerhouse.

The Zags had some creative young coaches – one who stayed through the building phases – an engaged administration, and a situation where they weren’t getting pounded by better-sourced programs every outing.

BSU, SDSU, Fresno State, etc., can turn into new rivals, and make for exciting games, but the challenge of rising to elite win totals is less daunting than it ever was for WSU.

Regardless of the new logo’s contention, if the Cougars can continue to be aggressive, modern and unapologetic, they might not need superhero energy after all.

Washington State.title: If my WSU and Pac-12 calculations are correct, you're going to see some serious stuff | CFB preview 2026
Washington State.summary:
Well, you’ve done it now Cougar Fan. You helped Doc Dennis Erickson get his 2004 Toyota Camry up to 88 miles per hour just as lighting hit the Bryan Hall Clock Tower on WSU’s campus.

You leapt forward into the future. How? I don’t know, watch Interstellar or Rick and Morty if you have questions about the science. The point is the year is 2041, and you’re here.

President Zendaya’s Public Funding for Newspaper Columnists Act sailed through Congress, so I’m still here, too.

I am sure you have lots of questions about the state of the world, whether AI took everyone’s jobs, and what crazy new flavors of Oreos exist in the future. No? You just want to know how the Cougs are doing?

Sigh, all right.

Well, the first thing to know is nobody uses TV anymore. Everyone watches the games on their Nvidia Goggles. Even in the stadium, it’s the craziest thing …

All right, all right. You want to hear about the team. But first, you’ve got to understand how we got to this point.

Around the time you left, people were so fed up with the state of college sports that Congress was getting involved. Broadly, people understood that constant transfers were destroying the ability of fans to form connections with specific players and that the endless money shower was at risk.

What happened over the next five years? Not much good. While the schools kept trying to establish consistent rules around transfers, they kept losing in court. Meanwhile, the mega franchises of the Big Ten and SEC conferences continued to tighten their grip on other institutions.

They gobbled up playoff and marquee TV spots year after year. This growing imbalance meant that when it came time for media negotiations, the remaining conferences – such as the rebuilt Pac-12 – were offered progressively worse deals.

The effect on Washington State University was particularly severe. The Pac-12’s second media deal, finalized in 2031, provided even less revenue than the agreement that began in 2026. That earlier deal was already a bitter pill, amounting to not much more than a third of what WSU used to make from football broadcasts after adjusting for inflation.

The SEC and Big Ten’s flirting and dancing around each other was finally consummated with the formation of a super conference in 2032. What’s more, they insisted their new mega conference – aptly titled the Monied Enemies Getting Along Conference – receive 22 automatic berths to the 24-team playoff.

Adding injury to insult, the MEGA Conference invited UNLV to join, leaving the Pac-12 kicking itself for passing on the chance to add a school from one of the country’s fastest growing regions and arguably its biggest hotspot for sports tourism.

Things seemed dire. What was a school like WSU to do?

Well, now that you mention it, on the field things didn’t really change that much. The rich schools could still only take so many players, and while homegrown Cougars stars would often leave if the money got to be too good, someone new would fill in just fine.

Iconic games and thrilling finishes led to new rivalries in the Pac-12, and while the money wasn’t as good, about the same number of people watched WSU take on Oregon State and Boise State as ever before.

Seeing an opportunity with so many schools locked out of the College Football Playoff, the TV Networks pitched an alternative season-ending tournament. Much like the NIT in college basketball for the schools who do not make the NCAA Tournament.

And much like the NIT when the NCAA Tournament was limited to a small number of teams, the alternative college football playoffs were really popular.

Cal and Stanford, seeing no benefit to flying across the country to face Atlantic Coast foes, finally came back home, joining the new Pac-12, which regularly sends teams to the finals of this National Football Tournament.

A year earlier, Nebraska shocked college football by announcing its intention to join the Pac-12, tired as the Cornhuskers are of finishing 20th or worse in the MEGA Conference.

There are more than a few rumors online that UW and UCLA may like to do the same, though the Pac-12 commissioner has already declared that any other former Pac-12 schools will need to accept half shares.

Anyway, it’s probably time for you to go back to your own time. If you need to get that old Camry up to speed, I recommend hijacking the new bullet train between Spokane and Pullman.

Washington State.title: Great Scott? Hardly. How reversing four moments in history might have saved the original Pac-12 | CFB preview 2026
Washington State.summary:
The Pac-12’s return from near-extinction is the inspired result of a harrowing process in which a handful of executives at the conference office, Washington State and Oregon State made all the right moves. In that regard, the rescue operation stands in stark contrast to the previous 12 years, when two bumbling commissioners, their coterie of acolytes and clueless university presidents did everything wrong.

It’s extraordinarily difficult to destroy a 100-year-old conference that produced the likes of Jackie Robinson, Tiger Woods, Ronnie Lott, Annika Sörenstam, Steve Prefontaine and Barry Bonds, not to mention Mr. William Theodore Walton.

In fact, survival hinged on a seemingly simple task. Given numerous off-ramps to tranquility throughout the 2010s and early 2020s, Pac-12 leaders instead led the conference down the path to implosion.

You know the endgame.

USC and UCLA left for the Big Ten in the summer of 2022. A year later, eight more schools headed for the exit, leaving Washington State and Oregon State adrift in the realignment seas for 13 months until the reclamation project eventually took shape.

Could changing a moment (or four) have preserved the original Pac-12, thus allowing the Cougars and Beavers to maintain their Power Five status and ensuring a competitive balance across the college athletics landscape?

Therein lies the waste, folks.

Had Pac-12 executives taken a different approach with just one strategic initiative during their decade of delusion – one out of a dozen! – the original conference would be intact today.

Here are four examples of failed strategy that led to the Pac-12’s implosion in August 2023.

Long and short of it

Former commissioner Larry Scott was lauded from coast to coast when he secured a 12-year, $3 billion media rights deal with Fox and ESPN in the spring of 2011, following the decision to add Utah and Colorado and create divisions.

The cash component soon lost luster as other major conferences signed more lucrative contracts. But the duration of Scott’s agreement proved downright disastrous for the Pac-12 because it locked in the schools until the summer of 2024. While the value of sports rights continued to soar in the 2010s, the schools were stuck in cement shoes, unable to return to the negotiating table to take advantage.

And sure enough, Scott was outmaneuvered.

In the spring of 2016, Big Ten commissioner Jim Delany finalized a media rights contract for his conference that lasted a mere six years, meaning it expired one year before the termination of the Pac-12’s deal.

That jumped the Big Ten in front of the Pac-12 in the contract cycle. With Fox’s backing, Delany’s successor, Kevin Warren, dangled an offer in front of USC and UCLA that they could not refuse.

Had Scott taken a shorter media deal initially – or had he built an opt-out provision into the original version – the Pac-12 could have returned to the negotiating table prior to the Big Ten in 2022 and secured an agreement that both increased the Pac-12’s revenue and prevented the L.A. schools from leaving.

Pac-12 Networks whiff

After signing with ESPN and Fox, Scott received approval from the presidents to create a media company wholly owned by the schools and install himself as the chief executive.

Launched in the fall of 2012, the Pac-12 Networks featured first-rate production, one national network and six regional feeds. But in both expanse and expense, the media company far exceeded the value of the content it delivered. The result was an ongoing struggle for distribution and revenue that would hinder the schools for 12 years.

The greatest whiff, of course, was not partnering with DirecTV – a fatal flaw rooted in the Pac-12 Networks’ business model.

DirecTV was willing to partner with the Pac-12, but only at a cheaper price than other carriers (e.g., Comcast) were paying. Because of the so-called “Most Favored Nation” clause in the distribution deals, Scott would have been forced to drop the subscription price for every carrier if he lowered the number for DirecTV, thereby wrecking what slim profits existed.

The Pac-12 Networks nightmare lasted 12 years, limiting exposure for the Pac-12’s most important export (football) and reducing the chief import (cash). Scott’s original financial projections showed $3 million per school (per year) as the bare minimum each campus could expect. Over time, that amount became the best-case scenario.

No school was more frustrated by the dearth of exposure and cash than USC.

Refusing ESPN’s lifeboat

In late 2018, ESPN approached Scott and offered to take over distribution of the Pac-12 Networks in exchange for a long-haul Tier 1 media rights deal, according to a report in the Sports Business Journal several months after the fact.

Scott and the presidents declined the lifeboat, preferring instead to maintain full control of the struggling networks under the presumption that the wholly-owned media company would eventually be worth a fortune.

As Arizona State president Michael Crow told 98.7 FM in Phoenix in early 2020: The Pac-12 Networks “will be unbelievably valuable as we move into this internet streaming world and people want to see the hundreds of live events we have.”

Of course, that jackpot never materialized. Quite the opposite, in fact: The networks became an anchor that eventually undermined the stability of the conference.

Had Scott and the presidents embraced ESPN’s offer, instead of clinging to their own distorted dreams, the resulting long-term contract would not have given USC and UCLA a path into the Big Ten. They would have been locked into the conference through the 2020s.

Expansion … or contraction

The summer of 2021 did not produce the final nail, but it was telling nonetheless.

In late July, Texas and Oklahoma made the first move in a wave of conference realignment that ripples to this day. Their announced departure from the Big 12 to the SEC left the former devastated and its remaining schools desperate for an escape hatch.

They called the Pac-12, but commissioner George Kliavkoff, who replaced Scott, and the university presidents determined that none of the Big 12 schools were good fits competitively, financially and institutionally.

Had the conference agreed to expand – not with all the Big 12 schools but with a handful, plus BYU – it would have been fortified against the L.A. thunderbolt that struck a year later.

In the realignment game, there is strength in numbers.

The final twist of the knife came when the Big 12, which survived only because its schools were not deemed worthy of membership in the Pac-12, rose up and raided its rival in that fateful summer of 2023.

Now here we are three years later, with the rebuilt conference preparing for its inaugural football season and the scars of implosion visible across the region.

Time after time, leaders of the former Pac-12 had off-ramps to salvation available.

Time after time, propelled by their own hubris, they kept speeding down the road to the abyss.

Washington State.title: How WSU is positioning itself to overcome challenging first year in new Pac-12 | CFB preview 2026
Washington State.summary:
Washington State’s era of new just keeps rolling on.

For the second straight year, there are a lot of updates around the Cougars program, from the top down. It’s the first year for head coach Kirby Moore, who comes over from Missouri, where he worked three years as offensive coordinator. It’s the first year for the reshuffled Pac-12. And it’s the first season for the Cougars’ crop of newcomers, who get the challenge of navigating it all.

How will WSU manage?

What’s clear about the Cougars’ season is this: They will open the season in only the most challenging of ways. WSU’s season-opener is a road matchup against rival Washington in the Apple Cup, the first to open the season in the programs’ history, and only six days later the Cougars get a road test at Kansas State. That game is set for 9 a.m.

WSU gets a bit of reprieve the following week, when FCS Duquesne comes to town, but things ramp back up the week after with a home tilt against former Pac-12 foe Arizona. Add it all up and it’s a grueling start to Moore’s first season, three Power 4 foes in less than four weeks’ time.

Those tales have yet to be told, which is why it can be difficult to gauge Moore’s mentality so far out. He can sound like a broken record, talking about daily improvement and taking things day-by-day, but there might be a method to it all.

“I wanna make sure everyone understands why we’re doing something, why we’re practicing at 11,” Moore said. “Why we’re doing this in the weight room, why we’re meeting at this time, because every decision should start with our players. I love our staff, but the players are gonna make plays out here on Saturday. No staff member is gonna make any plays.”

As far as the players go, there are several to keep an eye on. The Cougars’ starting quarterback will be UC Davis transfer Caden Pinnick, who put up an impressive redshirt freshman season with the Aggies: He completed 240 of 345 passes (70%) for 3,206 yards and 32 touchdowns against 10 interceptions, winning Big Sky Freshman of the Year honors. He also registered 125 carries for 437 yards and three scores, good for an average rush of 3.5 yards, underscoring his dual-threat capabilities.

Then there’s the Cougars’ running back trio of Kirby Vorhees, Maxwell Woods and Leo Pulalasi, all of whom decided to return to WSU in a key offseason development. Vorhees and Pulalasi flirted with the transfer portal – Vorhees announced he was planning to enter, while Pulalasi entered and later withdrew his name – but they will be wearing crimson and gray this fall, which is great news for the offensive-minded Moore. Look for all three to make a splash, and don’t be surprised if freshmen tailbacks Tre Hill Jr. or Marquez Wimberly get a few scattered carries.

Even so, if fall camp was any indication, the strength of this WSU team might be its defense. That unit earned the edge in just about every fall camp practice. Safety Jaylen Thomas snagged three interceptions, including two on Pinnick, while defensive end duo Matyus McLain (Idaho transfer) and Linus Zunk (Vanderbilt transfer) figure to terrorize all kinds of offensive lines this fall.

Flank those two around the Cougars’ defensive line, far and away the deepest position group on the team, and you start to see the problems the whole unit could cause opposing offenses. The Cougars’ interior starters will likely be returner Kaden Beatty and transfer Paul Hutson III, but look for pieces like SMU transfer Damarjhe Lewis, Eastern Washington transfer Jirah Leaupepetele and Saint Francis transfer Balaam Miller to earn key roles as well.

“Obviously, both coming over in their first year, have experience at the previous schools they were at, playing experience,” defensive ends coach Andrew Browning said of McLain and Zunk. “Being older too in the room. We have a relatively younger room in general. Those guys have acquainted themselves with their teammates really well, and they’ve been a really good lead-by-example. And I think probably the biggest thing I’ve noticed is they’ve found their voice a little bit within our group and within the defense, and that’s been really good to see.”

All that said, WSU hardly has an easy rest of the schedule, no matter how the first four games go. Perhaps most notably, their one bye week doesn’t arrive until after Week 9, after the Cougars’ road game against San Diego State. That game will be a real test, as will away games against Oregon State (Oct. 17) and Texas State (Nov. 21), a pick to finish in the top half of the new conference.

Can the Cougars withstand enough of those games to earn six wins and make a bowl game, which the program has done in nine of the last 10 full seasons? If so, it probably means that Pinnick made the transition from FCS football to FBS ball without a hitch, and that the Cougars’ defense established itself as one of the Pac-12’s finest units.

For a program that became famous for its offense, that development would register as new, too.

“I think I’m just always trying to find a better way to do things,” Moore said, “whether that’s probably life-related. Even our trainer, I was asking him a question about, you know, there’s some new studies out about, hey, you drink your coffee an hour later. It’s supposed to be better for you in the morning when you wake up. I think there’s football things. There’s meeting things. We’re teachers first. That’s what I grew up around. My mom was an elementary school principal. Dad was a high school football coach and a teacher. I think the head coaches that I’ve been around – there’s been a lot of really good ways to do things and making sure what’s the best fit for Washington State.”

Washington State.title: Making the case for a 5-7 WSU season sidetracked by difficult schedule | CFP preview 2026
Washington State.summary:
Sept. 6, 1 p.m. (NBC)

At Washington

Best case: With a chance to capitalize on a UW defense that doesn’t have much tape of the WSU offense, QB Caden Pinnick and RB Kirby Vorhees provide enough offense to let their defense do the rest.

Worst case:Pinnick shows his lack of FBS experience as the Huskies’ defense tees off on a Cougar offense that left something to be desired during fall camp.

Final: UW 24, WSU 10

Sept. 12, 9 a.m. (TNT)

At Kansas State

Best case: WSU’s pass rush torches an injury-riddled K-State offensive line, safety Jaylen Thomas snares an interception and the Cougs’ defense gives their offense a chance to eke out a win on the road.

Worst case:On a short week and an early kickoff time, WSU never generates much offense and limps to a second straight defeat to open the season.

Final: K-State 20, WSU 7

Sept. 19, 12:30 p.m. (USA Network)

Vs. Duquesne

Best case: Pinnick and the Cougars offense wakes up and demolishes Duquense’s defense, inspiring confidence among the team and fans leading into a showdown with Arizona the following week.

Worst case:A challenging open to the season wears down the Cougars, who don’t have the manpower to generate enough offense as the Dukes’ defense forces a pair of turnovers and stuns the hosts.

Final: WSU 27, Duquesne 3

Sept. 26, 4:30 p.m. (CBS)

Vs. Arizona

Best case: WSU’s defense limits veteran quarterback Noah Fifita and produces several turnovers, swinging the tide of the game in time for Pinnick and the Cougars’ offense to pull an upset at home.

Worst case:Pinnick and WSU’s offense never shows up, showing the unit’s limitations against an upper-tier Power 4 team and losing several costly turnovers.

Final: Arizona 23, WSU 20

Oct. 3, 6:30 p.m. (USA Network)

Vs. Fresno State

Best case: The Cougars’ swarming defense makes QB Khristian Martin pay for his inexperience, picking him off twice, and their ground game neutralizes star DB Simeon Harris to produce enough offense.

Worst case:Pinnick tests Harris once too many times, leading to a costly interception, and the Bulldogs show why they’re picked to finish near the top of the Pac-12.

Final: WSU 17, Fresno State 16

Oct. 9, 6 p.m. (The CW)

At Utah State

Best case: WSU capitalizes on a new and unproven Utah State defense, which can’t slow down Vorhees or running back Maxwell Woods before they run roughshod and help the Cougars cruise to a win.

Worst case:The Aggies’ new-look defense lets their home-field advantage fuel an upset, forcing critical turnovers on Pinnick and the Cougs’ offense.

Final: WSU 17, Utah State 14

Oct. 17, 3 p.m. (USA Network)

At Oregon State

Best case: Oregon State’s first campaign under new head coach Jamarcus Shepard continues to struggle as WSU uses a hellacious defensive effort to earn its first win in Corvallis since 2020.

Worst case:The ghosts of Reser Stadium continue to haunt the Cougars, whose offense falls apart when it matters most.

Final: Oregon State 22, WSU 17

Oct. 24, 3 p.m. (USA Network)

Vs. Boise State

Best case: WSU establishes a robust ground attack, taking star edge rusher Jayden Virgin-Morgan away from what he does best, and the Cougs’ pass rush flummoxes QB Maddux Madsen.

Worst case:Virgin-Morgan and Boise State’s defense hands WSU its worst offensive outing of the season, turning over Pinnick multiple times en route to a blowout win in the Broncos’ first trip to Pullman since 2017.

Final: Boise State 23, WSU 17

Oct. 31, 4 p.m. (CBS Sports Network)

At San Diego State

Best case: The Cougars’ offense roars to life against an unproven SDSU defense, which can’t contain Vorhees or Woods, shredding the Aztecs’ defense and helping the visitors earn their first signature road win in the Kirby Moore era.

Worst case:WSU suffers its first letdown on defense all season, unable to contain the SDSU tandem of QB Jayden Denegal and RB Lucky Sutton as the Aztecs cruise to an easy win.

Final: SDSU 24, WSU 12

Nov. 14, 7:30 p.m. (CBS Sports Network)

Vs. Colorado State

Best case: WSU secures an easy win over a rebuilding Colorado State squad, its offense hitting its stride and dismantling an inexperienced CSU defense, which can’t slow down Pinnick and Co.

Worst case:CSU QB Hauss Hejny shows why he originally landed at Oklahoma State, picking apart the middle of WSU’s defense, where linebackers DJ Warner and Keith Brown struggle to contain things.

Final: WSU 27, CSU 14

Nov. 21, 3 p.m. (USA Network)

At Texas State

Best case: Texas State’s defense is the question mark of the team, and WSU exposes it as such, getting a big game from WR Darrius Clemons as the Cougars escape with a stunner of a road win.

Worst case:Bobcat QB Brad Jackson uses a high-powered offense to carve up a WSU defense worn down by the grind of the season, stonewalling McLain and Zunk and handing the Cougs’ defense a list of ways to improve.

Final: Texas State 24, WSU 10

Nov. 28, time/TV TBD

Vs. Oregon State (FLEX)

Best case: With a chance to reflect on the teams’ first meeting in Corvallis, WSU demonstrates why its program is in a better place than the other traditional Pac-12 holdover, winning another game over the Beavers in Pullman.

Worst case:The Beavers’ offense wakes up and spoils the Cougars’ senior night, with QB Maalik Murphy enjoying his best game of the season.

Final: WSU 22, Oregon State 10

Washington State.title: Pac-12 forecast: Boise State a clear favorite, with WSU somewhere in the middle | CFB preview 2026
Washington State.summary:
Everything is set for the inaugural season of the rebuilt Pac-12, which returns to competition Labor Day weekend and begins intra-conference play Oct. 3.

How will it look seven short weeks later? This is how we see it:

1. Boise State

An easy call given the known commodities on both sides of scrimmage and, let’s not forget, the sideline. Third-year coach Spencer Danielson has the record (21-7), the culture and the personnel to claim yet another conference title (albeit in a different conference). The combination of veteran quarterback Maddux Madsen, big-play tailback Dylan Riley and a well-stocked defense make Boise State a threat to return to the College Football Playoff. All eyes will be on the season opener at Oregon, but we view the Week 2 home date with Memphis as a better indicator of Boise State’s playoff prospects.

2. Fresno State

Admittedly, this placement requires a leap of faith that second-year coach Matt Entz will coax and cajole enough efficiency from his QBs to allow the other units to thrive. Khristian Martin, a transfer from Maryland, is considered the frontrunner, but his inexperience suggests the learning curve could be steep, at least initially. The Bulldogs have perhaps the Pac-12’s best tailback in Rayshon Luke and are solid on every level of defense. Also, they get Boise State at home (Oct. 10) in what could shape the race.

3. Texas State

First, we’ll acknowledge the Bobcats are the most difficult team in the conference to project because of their transition from the Sun Belt – they are the outlier. That said, there is no doubting the quality of their quarterback play with the dynamic Brad Jackson, who accounted for 38 touchdowns last season, and a handful of proven receivers. A repeat performance from the playmakers seems necessary considering the retooled defensive line and secondary. All in all, we expect a bumpy start and strong finish for the Bobcats.

4. San Diego State

The Aztecs should field one of the conference’s most productive offenses with senior quarterback Jayden Denegal and star tailback Lucky Sutton. But the secondary was hit hard by attrition; the top edge rushers (Trey White and Ryan Henderson) are gone; and the departure of defensive mastermind Rob Aurich (to Nebraska) has not received enough attention from the prognosticating public. Will the regression on one side of scrimmage fully offset progress on the other? Probably not. But the Aztecs won’t have San Jose State, Nevada and Wyoming to beat up on, either.

5. Washington State

Give first-year coach Kirby Moore high marks for hiring former Oregon State boss Trent Bray to run WSU’s defense, and our hunch is that quarterback Caden Pinnick will manage the transition from UC Davis without much trouble. But there are enough questions about the skill-position talent and the defensive front to make us slightly wary of slotting the Cougars in the top half of the conference. Of course, the Hotline refuses to pick ties even though eight teams playing seven games likely will result in a logjam somewhere. For example: WSU could finish 4-3 and in a three-team tie for third.

6. Utah State

Our dim forecast for the Aggies begins at the beginning: Their non-conference schedule, with trips to Washington and Utah, could leave the depth chart battered and bruised when they commence Pac-12 play with … a trip to Boise State. And it’s not like coach Bronco Mendenhall will be sending a veteran lineup through that gauntlet, either. The Aggies are revamping several positions, including quarterback and the offensive line. A late-season surge is possible if the lineup isn’t decimated.

7. Oregon State

The Hotline hasn’t been wrong about anything in at least 90 seconds, and we could be completely misreading the state of play in Corvallis. But from here, Year 1 under coach JaMarcus Shephard looks grim. The schedule includes trips to Boise State and Fresno State; the lines of scrimmage look flawed; there are too few playmakers; and we have no idea what to make of the quarterback situation. There’s an old saying: When you have two quarterbacks, you really have no quarterbacks. Well, the Beavers have three.

8. Colorado State

In hiring Jim Mora, the Rams took exactly the type of calculated risk necessary to elevate their program at just the right time. But Mora’s roster includes more than 60 new players – many followed him from Connecticut – and there are enough unknowns that the Hotline is hesitant to project a brighter outlook. The list of uncertainties starts at QB, where Oklahoma State transfer Hauss Hejny is locked in a competition with K’saan Farrar, one of the UConn transplants.

CFP repeat for Oregon as WSU scrambles for six wins | Pac-12 (legacy) bowl forecast
Washington State.summary:
Bowl executives continue to treat the Pac-12 as though it never collapsed. For the third consecutive season, the 12 legacy schools spread across four conferences will be grouped together for the purpose of determining their postseason destinations.

And once again, the primary landing spots for teams that don’t qualify for the College Football Playoff will be the Alamo, Las Vegas, Holiday and Sun bowls.

The Independence is back in the rotation, as well. And the Poinsettia, in San Diego, is reportedly returning to action after a nine-year hiatus.

If that arrangement weren’t complicated enough, with the bowl tie-ins from 2023 in place for 2026, there’s an added complication. The Pac-12 reconstituted this summer with Washington State, Oregon State and six new teams, and some overlap exists with the bowl selection process.

For these projections, our focus will remain on the 12 legacy schools.

Here we go.

College Football Playoff

Team: Oregon

Comment: Only a fairly stunning sequence of events will prevent the Ducks from making their third consecutive appearance in the CFP. But the bar is higher than mere participation for Dan Lanning and Co., who were blown off the field by Ohio State two years ago and Indiana last season. Considering their loaded roster, the Ducks need to reach the championship game for the season to be considered an indisputable success.

Alamo Bowl

Team: Washington

Comment: The Huskies are one of several Pac-12 legacy teams with a realistic chance to make the CFP. Given the layout of their schedule, which starts soft and builds to a brutal finish, the Huskies must be at least 9-1 entering the final two games, then conjure a split against Indiana (home) and Oregon (road). From our vantage point, the roster isn’t quite talented enough to avoid multiple stumbles between early September and the middle of November. The Alamo (vs. the Big 12) would nonetheless constitute progress under third-year coach Jedd Fisch.

Las Vegas Bowl

Team: Arizona

Comment: Our forecast for the Wildcats, who would face an SEC or Big Ten foe in Las Vegas, is admittedly rosier than most. It’s based on the presence of an elite quarterback (Noah Fifita), coaching continuity, experience on the lines of scrimmage, proven playmakers and a manageable schedule. If that mix of ingredients were in place for USC, Utah, Washington or Oregon following a nine-win season, projections for the following fall would be glowing. But because of Arizona’s low football profile, national expectations are modest.

Holiday Bowl

Team: USC

Comment: What could be a make-or-break fifth season for Lincoln Riley features significant buzz, and with good reason. The Trojans retained quarterback Jayden Maiava, fortified the lines of scrimmage and employed the services of a defensive master, Gary Patterson, in order to upgrade a unit that has not functioned at a playoff-caliber level in the Riley era. Will that be enough for a CFP berth? USC needs to win at least three of five games against Oregon, Washington, Penn State, Ohio State and Indiana. That feels like a stretch, leading to a date in the Holiday against an ACC opponent.

Sun Bowl

Team: Utah

Comment: Our outlook for the first year of the Morgan Scalley era is slightly skeptical. But of this, we have no doubt: The schedule is built for eight wins. The Utes miss Texas Tech, play Houston and BYU at home and have only two tough road games (Arizona and TCU). If they win eight, the Holiday Bowl could come calling. We see the Sun Bowl (vs. the ACC) as their floor.

Poinsettia Bowl

Team: UCLA

Comment: Operated by the same folks who run the Holiday, the Poinsettia Bowl will match one of the 10 departed Pac-12 schools against a team from the new version of the conference (including Washington State and Oregon State). It stands as an obvious landing spot for one of the six- or seven-win teams that will inevitably emerge. The Bruins have a soft schedule and would offer the reborn bowl solid ticket-sale possibilities.

Independence Bowl

Team: Arizona State

Comment: The Independence returns to the rotation having last welcomed a Pac-12 representative in 2023 (Cal) and will match one of the legacy teams against the Big 12. The Sun Devils seem well-matched for a mid-level bowl like the Independence, or perhaps the Poinsettia, considering the uncertainty at quarterback and an arduous schedule. What’s more, they won’t be a candidate for the Sun, having participated last year, and the Holiday seems a tier too high.

ESPN bowl pool

Team: Cal

Comment: The Bears have not won more than seven games in the regular season since 2009, a remarkable stretch of mediocrity. Will first-year coach Tosh Lupoi create a new ceiling? We need to see it to believe it, especially with a schedule that offers little margin for error. The opener, against UCLA, is a whopper – not only because of the ongoing bitterness over the Bruins’ role in the demise of the Pac-12 but also because of the impact the result will have on each team’s bowl math.

ESPN bowl pool

Team: Washington State

Comment: No team possesses a wider range of outcomes than the Cougars, who could win the rebuilt Pac-12 and climb into the Holiday or Sun. Or they could stumble badly and be eliminated from the postseason in early November. The schedule doesn’t help matters, with three difficult nonconference games: Washington, Kansas State and Arizona. If they lose all three, the Cougars would need to win six of the remaining nine to become bowl-eligible.

Non-qualifier

Team: Colorado

Comment: There’s a path into the postseason for CU, but it requires high-level play from an inexperienced quarterback (Julian Lewis), dramatic improvement from what has been a subpar offensive line and expert coaching from a staff with two new coordinators. Bottom line: We aren’t convinced Deion Sanders can win without his son (Shedeur) at quarterback and a generational talent (Travis Hunter) playing both sides of scrimmage.

Non-qualifier

Team: Oregon State

Comment: Combine a first-year head coach (JaMarcus Shephard) with a new starting quarterback (Braden Atkinson, a transfer from Mercer) and a schedule that begins with Texas Tech and Houston – both are ranked in the AP preseason poll – and it seems likely that Oregon State will be playing from behind. Can the Beavers win six of their last 10, presuming they lose the Big 12 double-whammy? Not from where we sit.

Non-qualifier

Team: Stanford

Comment: Given the tepid state of the roster and the undeniable strength of the schedule, which includes four teams in the AP preseason poll (Miami, Notre Dame, Louisville and SMU), it’s difficult to envision the Cardinal reaching the six-win threshold for the first time since 2018. New coach Tavita Pritchard has a massive challenge ahead in order to make Stanford relevant in the next two or three years.
